method: Lectio Edition (SDIT): a synthesis of the full translation tradition — Samuel Butler (1900) and Butcher & Lang (1879) in the public domain, informed by the major modern renderings (Fitzgerald, Fagles, Wilson) as research and checked against the Greek. No copyrighted translation is reproduced; the rendering is original modern English. Reviewed for fidelity.
overview: The Lectio Edition tells the Odyssey in clear modern English, keeping the pace of the adventure and the warmth of the homecoming. Built from Butler’s public-domain prose and checked against the Greek, it aims to be as readable as Butler while restoring some of the poem’s music and the doubleness of its famously cunning hero.
introduction:
The Odyssey is the great poem of homecoming — ten years of one soldier's struggle to get back to his wife, his son, and his own small island after the Trojan War. Beneath the monsters and the gods it is about cunning, endurance, and the pull of home. This is the Lectio Edition — Homer in clear, living English, made to be read straight through.

The Greeks called Odysseus polytropos, "the man of many turns" — both far-traveled and quick-witted — and we keep that doubleness in the opening line. As in our Iliad, Homer's epithets (grey-eyed Athena, the wine-dark sea) are kept where they recur, and the gods and heroes keep their Greek names: Odysseus, not the Roman Ulysses; Athena, not Minerva. The rendering synthesizes the whole tradition — from Butler and Butcher–Lang through Fitzgerald, Fagles, and Wilson — checked against the Greek; it copies none of them.

divergences.older: “the man … never at a loss” (Butler); “for wisdom’s various arts renowned” (older verse)
divergences.lectio: “the man of many turns”
divergences.note: Polytropos literally means ‘of many turns’ — at once Odysseus’s much-wandering journey and his versatile, twisting cunning. Older versions pick one sense; Emily Wilson’s ‘complicated man’ keeps the doubleness. Lectio renders ‘the man of many turns’ to hold both.

divergences.older: “the much-enduring noble Odysseus”
divergences.lectio: “long-suffering Odysseus”
divergences.note: His standing epithet. Lectio keeps the key recurring epithets so the hero’s defining trait — endurance — stays audible, while modernising the phrasing.

divergences.older: “hospitality,” often unmarked
divergences.lectio: “guest-friendship,” with the idea drawn out
divergences.note: Xenia — the sacred bond between host and guest — is the moral engine of the whole poem, the thing the suitors violate and the Cyclops perverts. Lectio renders it so a modern reader feels it as the binding law it was, not mere good manners.

divergences.older: “she flew away in the form of an eagle” (Butler); “soars an eagle through the liquid skies” (Pope)
divergences.lectio: “gone in the form of a sea-eagle”
divergences.note: Homer doesn’t say plain eagle (aetos): the bird is a phēnē, a distinct large raptor — a sea-eagle or, by the lexicons, the bearded vulture (lammergeier). The older translators flatten it to “eagle”; Lectio keeps the rarer, sharper bird the Greek names, since the marvel that strikes Nestor is partly the strange, unmistakable form Athena takes.

divergences.older: “nine guilds with five hundred men in each” (Butler)
divergences.lectio: “nine companies seated there, five hundred men in each”
divergences.note: Hedrai means “seated divisions” — ranks of men at their places on the shore, not trade-guilds. Butler’s “guilds” imports a medieval institution; Lectio renders the plain image of nine seated companies, the way Cowper kept it as “ranges of seats.”

divergences.older: “show your mettle and make yourself a name in story” (Butler); “be what brave Orestes was before” (Pope)
divergences.lectio: “be a brave man, so that men yet unborn will speak well of you”
divergences.note: Nestor’s charge to Telemachus is blunt and direct — “be valiant” — with the Orestes story as the pointed example just spoken. Lectio keeps the plain imperative and the reach toward future generations (opsigonoi, “those born later”) rather than dressing it up.

divergences.older: “two great misfortunes which have fallen upon my house” (Butler)
divergences.lectio: “two evils that have come down on my house”
divergences.note: Telemachus numbers his grief: doia, “twofold” — first the lost father, then the suitors, a second evil he calls outright “worse.” Lectio keeps the plain count and the rising weight (the second is the greater), rather than smoothing the two into a single complaint, so the structure of the boy’s first public speech stays audible.

divergences.older: “a pall for the hero Laertes” (Butler); “a funeral robe” (Cowper)
divergences.lectio: “a shroud for the hero Laertes”
divergences.note: The cloth on Penelope’s loom is a pharos — a great woven sheet — marked taphēïon, “for burial.” Older versions soften it to “robe” or the dated “pall”; Lectio renders “shroud,” the plain word for the burial-cloth, so a modern reader feels exactly what the three-year trick was weaving and unweaving.

divergences.phrase: δρυψαμένω … παρειὰς ἀμφί τε δειράς (drupsamenō … pareias amphi te deiras)
divergences.older: “fighting fiercely and tearing at one another” (Butler); “they cuff, they tear” (Pope)
divergences.lectio: “they tore at each other with their talons — clawing each other’s cheeks and necks”
divergences.note: The Greek participle is dual and middle: the two eagles claw one another’s cheeks and necks, a sign of evenly matched slaughter, which is why Halitherses reads it as the suitors’ doom rather than a clean victory. Lectio keeps the reciprocity and the specific wounds the omen names.

divergences.older: "an herb that banishes all care, sorrow, and ill humour" (Butler); "a drug to lull all pain and anger" (older verse)
divergences.lectio: "a drug that quiets all pain and anger and brings forgetfulness of every sorrow"
divergences.note: Homer's word for Helen's Egyptian drug is nēpenthes — literally "no-grief" (nē-, not + penthos, grief/mourning), the root of the English word nepenthe. It is the poem's one named pharmaceutical, and its power is exact: not a vague tonic but a sorrow-killer so total that a man drugged with it could watch his own brother cut down and not weep. Lectio keeps the literal force — forgetfulness of grief — rather than Butler's softer "care and ill humour," since the horror Helen describes is the point.

divergences.older: "of amber" (Butler, footnoted as doubtful); "electrum" (literal)
divergences.lectio: "of gold and amber"
divergences.note: When Telemachus gapes at Menelaus' hall, Homer lists the gleam of bronze, gold, ēlektron, ivory, and silver. Ēlektron can mean either amber (the fossil resin, prized and traded from the north) or electrum (a pale gold–silver alloy). Lectio keeps "amber," the older and more concrete reading: the wonder is partly that this wealth has been gathered from the ends of the earth, and amber — carried down from the far north — names that reach better than a metallurgical alloy.

divergences.older: "Idothea, daughter to Proteus, the old man of the sea" (Butler)
divergences.lectio: "Eidothea, daughter of mighty Proteus, the old man of the sea"
divergences.note: The sea-nymph who betrays her shape-shifting father is Eidothea — Butler's "Idothea" drops the diphthong. Lectio restores the fuller Greek form. Her name and her father's both turn on shape: Proteus ("the first," but proverbially "the changeable one") becomes lion, serpent, leopard, boar, water, and tree before he yields the truth — the poem's image of how hard it is to pin a god down to a straight answer.

divergences.older: "jealous" (Butler, Butcher–Lang); "envious" (Pope, Cowper)
divergences.lectio: "grudging beyond all others"
divergences.note: Calypso's charge against the gods isn't romantic jealousy but a grudging double standard — gods may take mortal lovers, but begrudge a goddess the same. The matching verbs in her speech ("you grudge") confirm it. Lectio keeps the bitter, accusing sense the Greek carries, not the narrower "jealous."

divergences.older: "immortal" (often only the first half kept)
divergences.lectio: "deathless, never to grow old"
divergences.note: Calypso's offer is a two-part formula — not just deathless but ageless, exempt from the decay that makes ordinary immortality a curse. Lectio keeps both halves wherever the phrase recurs, since the un-aging is the whole point: she offers Odysseus what even the gods think no man should refuse.

divergences.older: "made him lose all memories of his sorrows" (Butler)
divergences.lectio: "to release him … from his bone-deep weariness"
divergences.note: Athena's gift of sleep at the book's end frees Odysseus from kamatos — physical toil and exhaustion, not grief. Butler embellishes it into forgetting his sorrows; the Greek (and the verse tradition) says only that she eases his crushing tiredness. Lectio keeps the plainer, truer sense: the man is simply spent.

divergences.older: "that man and wife should be of one mind in a house" (Butler); "the nuptial Union of the Mind" (Pope)
divergences.lectio: "the gift of one mind between you … of one heart and one mind"
divergences.note: The climax of Odysseus's famous blessing turns on a single coined word — homophrosynē, "same-mindedness," the deep accord of two people who think as one. It is the poem's quiet ideal of marriage, the thing Odysseus and Penelope have and the suitors can never imitate. Lectio keeps the literal force of the compound — one mind — rather than softening it to general harmony, since it is the standard against which the whole homecoming is measured.

divergences.older: "whether he should go up to her … and embrace her knees as a suppliant" (Butler)
divergences.lectio: "whether to clasp the lovely girl's knees and beg … and dare not touch your knees"
divergences.note: Greek supplication was physical: the suppliant grasped the protector's knees, binding them to mercy. Odysseus calculates — naked, salt-crusted, a stranger — that to seize the knees of a young unmarried girl would frighten and shame her, so he supplicates from a distance instead, and says so aloud ("I dare not touch your knees"). Lectio keeps the literal gesture and the tact of refusing it, since the whole scene is a masterclass in reading a situation: the cunning of Odysseus turned to courtesy.

divergences.older: "As the huntress Diana goes forth …"; "you are Jove's daughter Diana" (Butler)
divergences.lectio: "like Artemis the archer"; "most like Artemis, the daughter of great Zeus"
divergences.note: Butler, following the older convention, gives the Roman names — Diana, Jove, Neptune, Minerva, Vulcan. As throughout the Lectio Odyssey, we keep the Greek: Artemis, Zeus, Poseidon, Athena, Hephaestus, Apollo. The comparison to Artemis is exact and double-edged — she is the virgin huntress, tall and untouchable among her nymphs, which is precisely how Nausicaa stands among her maids, and precisely the line Odysseus must not cross.

divergences.phrase: Ἀρήτη … ὄνομ' ἐστὶν ἐπώνυμον (Arētē … onom' estin epōnymon)
divergences.older: “Her name is Arete, and she comes of the same family as her husband” (Butler); the wordplay dropped
divergences.lectio: the name kept as Arete, her excellence drawn out — “there is no better woman, in mind or in heart”
divergences.note: Homer says Arete's name is epōnymon — a “name to match,” sounding on aretē (excellence) and on the verb araomai (to pray, to be prayed-for): she is both the excellent one and the one suppliants pray to. The pun can't survive in English without renaming her, which the edition won't do. Lectio keeps the Greek name and lets the surrounding lines carry the sense the name carries — which is also why Athena tells Odysseus to fall at her knees first.

divergences.phrase: ἀθανάτους ὄντας καὶ ἀγήρως (athanatous ontas kai agērōs)
divergences.older: “so they were immortal and could never grow old” (Butler)
divergences.lectio: “deathless, and never to grow old, for all their days”
divergences.note: The gold and silver watchdogs Hephaestus forged carry the same two-part formula — deathless and ageless — that Calypso offered Odysseus in Book 5 (athanaton kai agēraon). Lectio renders it the same way each time it recurs, so the reader hears the echo: the very gift the man refused from a goddess is here cast in metal at a king's door.

divergences.older: “I wish you would stay here, marry my daughter, and become my son-in-law” (Butler)
divergences.lectio: “take my daughter to wife, and be called my son-in-law … But against your will, no Phaeacian shall keep you — Zeus forbid it”
divergences.note: Alcinous offers a kingdom and his daughter in nearly the same breath that he promises to send Odysseus home. Lectio keeps both halves and their order intact — the lavish offer, then the immediate guarantee that it binds nothing — since the restraint is the measure of the man and the safety of the scene: the Phaeacians honor a guest's will above their own wishes, the very law the suitors back home are trampling.

divergences.phrase: νεῖκος Ὀδυσσῆος καὶ Πηλεΐδεω Ἀχιλῆος (neikos Odysseos kai Pelēïdeo Achilēos)
divergences.older: "the quarrel between Ulysses and Achilles" (Butler); "the strife of Ithacus and Peleus' son" (older verse)
divergences.lectio: "the quarrel between Odysseus and Achilles … and the savage words they had hurled at each other"
divergences.note: Demodocus' first song is a lost quarrel-tale, and Homer's word is neikos — a flyting, a contest of words, not a feud of arms. The point is that the Greeks once fought with their tongues; Lectio keeps the verbal sting (the savage words) rather than flattening it to a vague "quarrel," so the reader feels why Agamemnon was glad to watch his two best men go at each other.

divergences.phrase: ἀμφ’ Ἄρεος φιλότητος ἐϋστεφάνου τ’ Ἀφροδίτης (amph’ Areos philotētos eüstephanou t’ Aphroditēs)
divergences.older: "the loves of Mars and Venus … defiled King Vulcan's marriage bed" (Butler, with the comedy primmed)
divergences.lectio: the song of Ares and Aphrodite kept franker, lighter, faster — Roman names restored to the Greek (Ares, Aphrodite, Hephaestus, Hermes)
divergences.note: Butler renders the gods by their Roman names and tightens his lips on the comedy, turning a broad Olympian farce into a Victorian scandal. The Greek is plainer and funnier: Hermes' open wish to lie under the chains beside golden Aphrodite is a joke, and the gods' helpless laughter is the song's whole engine. Lectio keeps the Greek names — as throughout our Odyssey — and lets the comedy move at the speed Homer gives it.

divergences.phrase: χαῖρε, ξεῖν’, ἵνα καί ποτ’ ἐὼν ἐν πατρίδι γαίῃ μνήσῃ ἐμεῖ’ (chaire, xein’ … mnēsēi emeu)
divergences.older: "Farewell stranger, do not forget me when you are safe at home again" (Butler); "think on me" (older verse)
divergences.lectio: "Farewell, stranger … remember me sometimes, for it is to me, first of all, that you owe the price of your life."
divergences.note: Nausicaa's last words to Odysseus are a single imperative, mnēsēi — "remember me" — spoken quietly at the pillar, the only farewell she is allowed in the whole poem. Lectio keeps the bareness of it; the restraint is the heartbreak. The phrase she uses for what he owes her — zōagria, the ransom paid for a life spared in battle — is rendered "the price of your life," since she is claiming, with a girl's pride and dignity, that she is the one who brought him back from the dead.

divergences.phrase: Οὖτις / μή τις / μῆτις (Outis / mē tis / mētis)
divergences.older: "Noman" (Butler, Pope, Cowper); "Nohbdy" (Fitzgerald)
divergences.lectio: "Nobody" — kept the same in the cave and in the giant's cry to his neighbors
divergences.note: Odysseus's masterstroke is a pun no English can fully carry. He names himself Outis, "Nobody." So when the other Cyclopes ask who is hurting Polyphemus and he roars "Nobody is killing me!" they shrug and leave. But Greek hides a second joke: the negative shifts to mē tis ("no one"), which sounds like mētis — "cunning," the very thing that has beaten the giant. Homer seals it himself: "my name and my flawless cunning had fooled them." Lectio keeps the plain English "Nobody" so the surface trick lands cleanly, and lets the line about cunning carry the buried pun, rather than respelling the name.

divergences.older: "Jove," "Neptune," and the Roman names (Butler, following the old convention)
divergences.lectio: Zeus, Poseidon, Apollo — and "Odysseus," never "Ulysses"
divergences.note: As everywhere in the Lectio Odyssey, we keep the Greek names against Butler's Roman ones. This matters more here than anywhere: the whole book turns on Zeus as the god of guests and suppliants — the law the Cyclops flouts — and on Poseidon, whose son Polyphemus is, and whose curse on Odysseus's homecoming drives the rest of the epic. The Roman masks would blur the family quarrel that the poem is built on.

divergences.older: "lawless and inhuman" (Butler), often unmarked elsewhere
divergences.lectio: "lawless," tied to the broken law of guest-friendship
divergences.note: The Cyclopes are athemistoi — literally "without themis," outside the divine and customary law that binds civilized men, above all the sacred bond of host and guest (xenia). The word is the moral pivot of the book: Polyphemus eats the very guests Zeus commands him to protect. Lectio keeps "lawless" sounding through the whole episode — in the people, in the monster, in Odysseus's taunt — so a modern reader feels it as the charge it is, not as mere wildness.

divergences.older: "the gods call it Moly" (Butler); "the plant the gods call Moly" (older verse)
divergences.lectio: the name kept as moly, with the divine etymology drawn out — "The gods call it moly. It is hard for mortal men to dig — but the gods can do anything."
divergences.note: Moly is the one named drug of power in the whole Odyssey — black at the root, milk-white at the flower, the herb Hermes pulls from the ground to make Odysseus spell-proof against Circe. Homer marks it as a word from the gods' own language ("the gods call it moly"), which is why mortals can barely uproot it. Lectio keeps the Greek name untranslated — there is no English for it, and the strangeness is the point — and preserves the note that it is the gods' word, not men's.

divergences.older: "he flayed me a prime ox-hide to hold the ways of the roaring winds" (Butler); "a bag … the skin of an ox" (older verse)
divergences.lectio: "He flayed the hide of a nine-year-old ox and made it into a bag, and into that bag he bound the ways of the howling winds"
divergences.note: Aeolus's gift is an askos — a wineskin or leather bag — made from the hide of an ox nine years old (enneōros), the exact age Homer gives. Butler keeps "prime ox-hide" but drops the number; the verse tradition keeps the bag and loses the precision of the age. Lectio restores the nine-year ox, the small concrete detail that marks the bag as a thing of value and craft — and keeps it a bag, not a vague "sack," since the crew's fatal mistake is that they take it for a treasure-bag of gold.

divergences.phrase: Τηλέπυλος … ἐγγὺς γὰρ νυκτός τε καὶ ἤματός εἰσι κέλευθοι (Tēlepylos … the paths of night and day lie near)
divergences.older: "where the shepherd … salutes him who is driving out his flock … they work much the same by night as they do by day" (Butler)
divergences.lectio: "a herdsman driving his flocks in at dusk calls out to a herdsman driving his out … A man who could go without sleep might earn double wages there … for the paths of the night and the day lie near each other."
divergences.note: The land of the Laestrygonians is a place of almost no night — the in-coming and out-going shepherds pass each other and trade calls because the dark is so short, and a sleepless man could draw two wages. The detail is one of Homer's strangest, a glimpse of the far north where the days run long, and Telepylus itself means roughly "far gates" or "wide gates." Lectio keeps the eerie near-touching of night and day exactly rather than flattening it to "they work by night as by day," because the strangeness is information — these are the edges of the known world, where the rules of the sky themselves bend.

divergences.phrase: βουλοίμην κ' ἐπάρουρος ἐὼν θητευέμεν ἄλλῳ (bouloimēn k' eparouros eōn thēteuemen allōi)
divergences.older: "I would rather be a paid servant in a poor man's house and be above ground than king of kings among the dead" (Butler); "a slave to the meanest hind" (older verse)
divergences.lectio: "I would rather be a hired hand, working another man's land — a man with no portion of his own, scraping by — and be alive, than be lord over all the wasted dead."
divergences.note: Achilles' famous reversal of his own Iliad creed. The Greek is precise: a thēs eparouros — a hired field-hand bound to another man's soil — serving an anēr aklēros, a man with no land-allotment of his own, the lowest free wage-earner in the Greek world, below even a small farmer. It is not quite "slave" (the man Achilles imagines is free, just landless and poor) and not quite Butler's vague "paid servant." Lectio keeps the exact social rung, because the whole force of the line is the distance fallen: the greatest of heroes would trade kingship over all the dead for the meanest living wage under the sun. Better the poorest life than the grandest death.

divergences.phrase: σκιῇ εἴκελον ἢ καὶ ὀνείρῳ (skiēi eikelon ē kai oneirōi)
divergences.older: "each time she flitted from my embrace as it were a dream or phantom" (Butler)
divergences.lectio: "three times she slipped through my hands like a shadow, like a dream"
divergences.note: Three times Odysseus lunges to hold his mother, and three times she escapes "like a shadow, like a dream" (skiē, shadow; oneiros, dream). The doubled simile is one of the poem's quietest, most devastating images of what death is — not a place but a loss of substance. Lectio keeps both halves of the comparison and the bare repetition of "three times," since the failure to embrace is the emotional center of the whole descent.

divergences.phrase: ἀλλ' ἀκέων ἀπὸ νόσφι (all' akeōn apo nosphi) — Ajax's silence
divergences.older: "He would not answer, but turned away to Erebus and to the other ghosts" (Butler)
divergences.lectio: "He gave me not one word in answer, but turned and went off into Erebus, to join the other spirits of the dead."
divergences.note: Ajax, who killed himself in shame after losing the contest for Achilles' armor to Odysseus, is the one ghost who will not speak. His silence — refusing the very words that might have eased the grudge — was singled out in antiquity (Longinus among them) as more eloquent than any speech. Lectio keeps it spare and lets the silence land: no embellishment, no softening, because the point is precisely the word Ajax withholds.

divergences.phrase: ἴδμεν γάρ τοι πάνθ' … ἴδμεν δ' ὅσσα γένηται (idmen … idmen, "we know … we know")
divergences.older: "he who listens will go on his way not only charmed, but wiser" (Butler); "sweet song" foregrounded (older verse)
divergences.lectio: the Sirens' lure rendered as knowledge — "we know everything the Greeks and the Trojans suffered … and we know all that happens anywhere on the fruitful earth"
divergences.note: The Sirens' bait is not mere sweetness but omniscience: the Greek hammers the verb idmen, "we know," twice, and what they offer is the whole truth of Troy and of everything on earth — exactly the knowledge a man like Odysseus cannot resist. Older translations lean on the beauty of the voice and soften the claim to a vague "wiser"; Lectio keeps the doubled "we know" and the specific offer, since the deadliness of the song is that it promises understanding, not just pleasure.

divergences.older: "the Wanderers" (Butler); Roman "Jove," "Juno," "Neptune," "Amphitrite" (Butler)
divergences.lectio: "the Wandering Rocks"; the Greek gods kept — Zeus, Hera, the Earthshaker, Amphitrite
divergences.note: Circe lays out two roads, and Lectio keeps the names the Greek gives. The Planktai are "the Wandering Rocks," the route the Argo alone survived; against Butler's Roman masks the gods stay Greek — Father Zeus whose doves the rock snatches, Hera who saw the Argo through for love of Jason, the Earthshaker Poseidon who could not save a man caught in Charybdis. The naming matters because the same divine quarrel that drives the whole poem runs through this passage.

divergences.phrase: οἴκτιστον δὴ κεῖνο ἐμοῖσ' ἴδον ὀφθαλμοῖσι (oiktiston … the most pitiful thing I saw)
divergences.older: "the most sickening sight that I saw throughout all my voyages" (Butler)
divergences.lectio: "the most pitiful thing my eyes ever saw in all my wanderings on the paths of the sea"
divergences.note: When Scylla swings the six men up to her cave and they scream Odysseus's name, he calls it oiktiston — the most pitiable, most grief-stirring sight of all his sufferings, sealed by the long simile of the fisherman flinging little fish gasping onto the rocks. Butler's "sickening" tilts it toward disgust; the Greek word is pity, the helpless grief of a captain watching his best men die and unable to lift a hand. Lectio keeps the bareness of the fisherman simile and renders the verdict as pity, since the horror here is sorrow, not revulsion.

divergences.phrase: ὕπνος … νήγρετος ἥδιστος, θανάτῳ ἄγχιστα ἐοικώς (hypnos … nēgretos hēdistos, thanatōi anchista eoikōs)
divergences.older: “a deep, sweet, and almost deathlike slumber” (Butler); “sweet sleep … most like to death” (older verse)
divergences.lectio: “a deep, sweet, unbroken sleep, the very likeness of death”
divergences.note: As the Phaeacian ship pulls away, Homer marks Odysseus’s sleep with three exact words — nēgretos (“unwakable,” not to be roused), hēdistos (“sweetest”), and the open comparison thanatōi anchista eoikōs, “coming nearest to death.” It is the most lavishly described sleep in the poem, and the doubleness is the point: the homecoming is sweet, yet the crossing carries him over the water unconscious as a corpse, a man ferried home as the dead are ferried. Butler’s “almost deathlike” softens it; Lectio keeps all three notes — unbroken, sweet, and the bare likeness to death — since the strangeness of being carried home asleep, like a thing already gone, is the threshold the whole second half of the poem opens from.

divergences.phrase: κερδαλέος κ’ εἴη καὶ ἐπίκλοπος … κέρδεα (kerdaleos k’ eiē kai epiklopos … kerdea)
divergences.older: “He must be indeed a shifty lying fellow … we can both of us deceive upon occasion” (Butler); “we both know sharp practice” (older verse)
divergences.lectio: “We are two of a kind, you and I, both old hands at this”
divergences.note: When Athena drops her disguise she does not scold Odysseus for lying — she delights in it. The Greek calls him kerdaleos and epiklopos (“canny” and “thievish,” both edged with grudging admiration), and then she draws the line that makes them partners: of all mortals he is the best at plans and words, and she is foremost among the gods for mētis. The closing claim is mutual — they both know kerdea, the art of cunning advantage. Lectio renders the kinship plainly — “two of a kind … both old hands at this” — because the scene is the warm center of their whole alliance: the goddess loving the hero precisely for the trait other gods would punish, recognizing her own craft in his.

divergences.phrase: λᾶαν θῆκε … ὁ δ’ ἐρρίζωθη (laan thēke … ho d’ errhizōthē)
divergences.older: “turned it into stone, and drove it down with the flat of his hand so as to root it in the ground” (Butler)
divergences.lectio: “struck her flat with the palm of his hand, and rooted her where she stood, turned all to stone”
divergences.note: Poseidon’s revenge on the Phaeacians is one of the poem’s eeriest images: he does not sink the homing ship but petrifies it in sight of the harbor, still in the shape of a ship, with a single downward stroke of his hand that roots it (errhizōthē, “it took root”) like a thing grown out of the sea-floor. Lectio keeps the verb’s force — rooted, not merely fixed — and the flat blow of the palm, because the horror for the watching Phaeacians is exactly that the swift ship they prized becomes a dead stone landmark, the visible price of the kindness Poseidon will not forgive. The threatened mountain over the city is left as a threat, as the Greek leaves it: Alcinous’s vow to give no more escorts is the people’s attempt to buy it off.

divergences.phrase: τὸν δ' ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφης, Εὔμαιε συβῶτα (ton d' apameibomenos prosephēs, Eumaie subōta)
divergences.older: "To this you answered, O swineherd Eumaeus" (Butler, who keeps it); "Eumaeus, thou didst answer" (older verse, often dropped)
divergences.lectio: "And you answered him, Eumaeus, swineherd"
divergences.note: Five times in this book Homer breaks his own narration to speak to Eumaeus in the second person — "and you answered" — the only character in the whole Odyssey he addresses this way. Scholars read it as a mark of affection for the poem's one wholly faithful servant, a closeness the third person would lose. Lectio keeps the apostrophe each time it recurs rather than flattening it to "Eumaeus answered," since the intimacy is the point.

divergences.phrase: πρὸς γὰρ Διός εἰσιν ἅπαντες ξεῖνοί τε πτωχοί τε (pros gar Dios eisin hapantes xeinoi te ptōchoi te)
divergences.older: "all strangers and beggars are from Jove" (Butler)
divergences.lectio: "every stranger, every beggar, comes to us from Zeus"
divergences.note: Eumaeus's creed, and the moral heart of the book: the stranger and the beggar are under Zeus's own protection, so to dishonor them is to offend the god — the law of guest-friendship (xenia) that the suitors trample and that this poor swineherd, who has almost nothing, keeps without fail. Lectio restores the Greek name Zeus for Butler's Roman "Jove," as throughout this Odyssey, and keeps the bare, doubled force — stranger and beggar alike — rather than softening it.

divergences.phrase: ἐκ μὲν Κρητάων γένος εὔχομαι … νόθον (ek men Krētaōn genos euchomai … nothon)
divergences.older: "I am by birth a Cretan … the son of a slave whom he had purchased for a concubine" (Butler)
divergences.lectio: "I am a Cretan by birth … the son of a bought woman, a slave he kept for his bed"
divergences.note: Odysseus's great false tale begins with a precise, plausible lie: he is a Cretan nothos — a base-born son, the child of a bought concubine, set level with the true-born sons by a generous father but cheated of his inheritance when the father died. The detail is what makes the lie convincing; it is the life of a real soldier of fortune. Lectio keeps the exact social fact (the bought slave-mother, the bastard's thin share) plainly, since the whole art of the scene is how true the false story sounds.

books.label: Book I
books.title: Athena Visits Ithaca
paragraphs: Tell me, Muse, of the man of many turns — the one who wandered far and long after he sacked the holy city of Troy. He saw the cities of many peoples and learned how they thought; he suffered deep grief on the open sea, fighting for his own life and for the safe homecoming of his men. But he could not save them, hard as he tried — they died by their own reckless folly, those fools, when they devoured the cattle of Hyperion the Sun, who took from them the day of their return. Of these things, goddess, daughter of Zeus, begin where you will, and tell us too.

By now everyone who had escaped a violent death — in the war or on the sea — was home. Only Odysseus was still kept from his wife and his own country, held back by the nymph Calypso, a queen among goddesses, who wanted him for a husband and kept him deep inside her hollow cave. And when at last, as the years rolled on, the time came that the gods had spun for him to return to Ithaca, his trials were still not over, not even among his own people. The gods pitied him now — all of them but Poseidon, who stayed furious with godlike Odysseus and would not let him reach his homeland.

But Poseidon had gone off to the distant Ethiopians — the Ethiopians who live at the ends of the earth, split in two, half toward the setting sun and half toward the dawn — to accept a great offering of bulls and rams, and there he sat, enjoying the feast. The rest of the gods, meanwhile, gathered in the halls of Olympian Zeus. And the father of gods and men spoke first, for his mind was on Aigisthos, on noble Aigisthos whom Agamemnon's son, far-famed Orestes, had killed. With that in mind, he spoke out to the immortals:

"It's a marvel — how mortals are forever blaming the gods. They say their troubles come from us, when in fact it's their own reckless folly that brings them grief beyond their share. Look at Aigisthos. He took Agamemnon's lawful wife for himself and killed the man when he came home — and he knew it would destroy him, because we warned him. We sent Hermes, the keen-eyed slayer of Argos, to tell him: don't kill the man, don't court his wife, because Orestes will come for vengeance once he's grown and longs for his own land. Hermes told him this for his own good — but he wouldn't listen. And now he has paid for it, all at once, in full."

Then grey-eyed Athena answered him: "Father of us all, son of Kronos, highest of the mighty — that man got exactly what he deserved, and so should anyone who does what he did. But it's not Aigisthos I'm thinking of. My heart aches for Odysseus, that wise, unlucky man, kept so long from everyone he loves on a lonely island ringed by the sea, the very navel of the waters. It's a wooded island, and a goddess lives there — daughter of cruel Atlas, who knows the depths of every sea and holds up by himself the great pillars that keep the earth and sky apart. His daughter holds that grieving, broken man, and works on him day after day with soft, coaxing words to make him forget Ithaca. But Odysseus, longing only to see the smoke rising from his own land, wants to die. And still your heart doesn't turn, Olympian. Didn't Odysseus please you, sacrificing beside the Greek ships on the wide plain of Troy? Why are you still so set against him, Zeus?"

And Zeus who gathers the clouds answered her: "My child, what a thing to let past your lips. How could I ever forget godlike Odysseus? No mortal alive has a finer mind, and no one has given more generously to the immortal gods who hold the wide heavens. No — it's Poseidon who circles the earth who keeps up this relentless rage, all because of the Cyclops whose eye Odysseus blinded: Polyphemos, mightiest of them all, son of Poseidon by the nymph Thoosa, daughter of Phorkys, lord of the restless sea. Ever since Odysseus put out his eye, Poseidon the earthshaker won't kill him, but drives him wandering far from home. Still — let all of us put our heads together and find him a way back. Poseidon will have to let his anger go. He can't hold out alone, against the will of every god."

Then grey-eyed Athena answered him: "Father of us all, son of Kronos, highest of the mighty — if it truly pleases the blessed gods now that wise Odysseus should come home, then let us send Hermes the runner, the slayer of Argos, to the island of Ogygia, to tell the lovely-haired nymph straight out what we've decided: that long-suffering Odysseus is to set out for home. As for me, I'll go down to Ithaca, to put fresh heart into his son. I'll fill him with courage, call the long-haired Greeks to assembly, and have him speak his mind to the suitors — those men forever slaughtering his crowded flocks and his shambling, twist-horned cattle. And I'll send him to Sparta and to sandy Pylos to ask after his dear father's homecoming, so the world may speak well of him."

So she spoke, and she bound beneath her feet the beautiful sandals, immortal and golden, that carry her over the water and the endless earth as fast as the wind. And she took up her heavy spear, tipped with sharp bronze — massive, solid, strong, the spear with which she breaks the ranks of warriors who cross her, the goddess and daughter of a mighty father. Down from the peaks of Olympus she swept, and stood in Ithaca at the gate of Odysseus' courtyard, on the threshold of the hall, the bronze spear in her hand — taking the form of a guest-friend, Mentes, the lord of the Taphians. There she found the proud suitors, sprawled on the hides of oxen they themselves had killed and eaten, amusing themselves with their game of counters in front of the doors. Heralds and quick servants worked around them — some mixing wine and water in the bowls, some wiping the tables down with their sponges and setting them out again, others carving up great portions of meat.

Godlike Telemachus saw her long before anyone else. He had been sitting among the suitors, sick at heart, picturing his noble father — how he might come back from somewhere and scatter these men through the house, and win back his own honor and rule his own estate. Lost in that thought among them, he caught sight of Athena and went straight to the gate, stung that a stranger had been left standing there at the door. He came up close, took her right hand, lifted the bronze spear from her, and spoke to her with winged words: "Welcome, stranger. You'll be treated kindly here. Eat first, and then tell us what you need."

With that he led the way, and Pallas Athena followed. When they were inside the high-roofed hall, he carried her spear to the tall pillar and set it in the polished rack, among the many spears of long-suffering Odysseus. Then he led her to a chair and seated her there, spreading a fine cloth beneath her, with a footstool under her feet. He drew up an inlaid bench for himself beside her, apart from the suitors, so his guest wouldn't be sickened by the racket of those arrogant men and lose his appetite — and so he could ask, in private, about his absent father.

A maid came with water in a beautiful golden pitcher and poured it over their hands into a silver basin, and drew up a polished table beside them. A grave housekeeper brought bread and laid it out, and many good things besides, giving freely from her stores. A carver lifted platters of every kind of meat and set them down, and placed golden cups beside them, while a herald came round again and again to fill the cups with wine.

Then the proud suitors came in. One by one they took their seats on the chairs and benches. Heralds poured water over their hands, serving women heaped the baskets with bread, and young men filled the bowls to the brim with wine. The men reached out for the good things spread before them, and when they'd had their fill of food and drink, their hearts turned to other things — to song and dancing, the crowning glories of a feast. A herald put a beautiful lyre into the hands of Phemios, who sang for the suitors against his will. He struck the strings and lifted his voice in a lovely song — and just then Telemachus leaned in close to grey-eyed Athena, his head near hers, so the others wouldn't hear, and said:

"Dear guest, I hope you won't take offense at what I'm about to say. These men have it easy — music and song, all of it free, because they're eating up another man's living, a man whose white bones are lying somewhere in the rain, rotting on dry land or rolling in the surf of the sea. If they ever saw him set foot in Ithaca again, every one of them would pray for faster legs instead of more gold — gold couldn't save them. But he's gone, lost to some cruel fate, and there's no comfort left for us, even when someone on earth claims he's still coming. The day of his return is dead. Now tell me this, honestly — who are you? Where do you come from? Where is your city, your family? What ship brought you here, and what crew? How did they bring you to Ithaca, and who did they say they were? You surely didn't come on foot. And tell me the truth: are you new to this house, or were you a friend of my father's? Many men came to our door, for he was a man who got around among people, in his time."

Then grey-eyed Athena answered him: "I'll tell you, and I'll tell you straight. I am Mentes, son of wise Anchialos, and I rule the Taphians, who love their oars. I've come ashore here with my ship and crew, sailing the wine-dark sea toward men of a foreign tongue — to Temesa, for copper, with a cargo of gleaming iron to trade. My ship is moored away from the town, off in the open country, in the harbor of Rheithron, under wooded Mount Neion. As for us, we're guest-friends from way back, on our fathers' side — go and ask the old hero Laertes, if you like. They tell me he doesn't come to town anymore, but lives out in the country, suffering, with one old serving woman to set out his food and drink whenever the weariness drags at his limbs from hauling himself up and down his vineyard slope. I came because they said your father was home at last — but it seems the gods are still blocking his road. Brilliant Odysseus is not dead, not yet, somewhere on this wide earth. He's alive, held back on some sea-ringed island in the middle of the deep, in the hands of rough, savage men who keep him there against his will. But let me tell you what the gods put into my heart — and I believe it will come true, though I'm no prophet and read no clear omen in birds. He won't be away from his own land much longer. Even bound in iron chains, that man would find a way home — he's that full of cunning. But tell me this, honestly: are you really Odysseus' son, big as you are now? You look so like him about the head and the fine eyes — for we two met often, before he sailed for Troy, where the bravest of the Argives went in their hollow ships. Since then, neither of us has laid eyes on the other."

And thoughtful Telemachus answered her: "I'll tell you the truth, stranger. My mother says I'm his son — but I don't know it for myself. No man ever really knows his own father. I only wish I were the son of some lucky man who grew old among his own possessions. As it is, they tell me I come from the unluckiest man ever born — and since you ask, that's my answer."

Then grey-eyed Athena said: "Surely the gods haven't doomed your line to vanish without a name — not while Penelope brings such a son as you into the world. But tell me this, honestly: what is this feast, this whole crowd? What do you need with it? Is it a banquet, a wedding? It's clearly no meal where each man pays his share — they swagger through the house so insolently, gorging themselves. Any decent man walking in on all this disgrace would be sick at the sight."

And thoughtful Telemachus answered her: "Stranger, since you ask me — once, while that man was still among us, this house was rich and honorable. But the gods turned against us and willed otherwise, and they have made him vanish more completely than any man before him. I wouldn't grieve even his death so much, if he had gone down with his men in the land of the Trojans, or died in the arms of his friends once the fighting was done. Then all the Greeks would have raised a mound over him, and he'd have won great glory for his son to inherit. Instead the storm-winds snatched him away, no glory, no trace — gone, leaving me nothing but grief and weeping. And it isn't only him I mourn for; the gods have piled other miseries on me besides. Every lord with power in the islands — in Doulichion, in Same, in wooded Zakynthos — and every man of rank in rocky Ithaca itself is courting my mother and wasting my house. She won't refuse the hateful marriage outright, but she can't bring herself to end it either. And so they devour my living, and soon enough they'll tear me apart as well."

Then Pallas Athena answered, stirred with anger: "It's a shameful thing — how badly you need Odysseus home, to lay his hands on these brazen suitors. If only he could come now and stand at the outer gate of his house — helmet on, shield and two spears in hand, the man he was when I first saw him in our halls, drinking and enjoying himself! He'd come back then from Ephyra, from the house of Ilos son of Mermeros, where he'd gone in his fast ship to beg a deadly poison to smear on his bronze-tipped arrows. Ilos wouldn't give it to him, out of fear of the everlasting gods, but my father gave him some, he loved him so. If only that Odysseus could meet these suitors now — every one of them would find a quick death and a bitter wedding.

"But that, of course, lies on the knees of the gods — whether he comes back and takes his revenge in his own halls, or not. What I urge you to think about now is how to drive these suitors out of the house. So listen, and take what I say to heart. Tomorrow morning call the Greek heroes to assembly, speak your mind to them all, and let the gods be your witnesses. Tell the suitors to scatter, each to his own home. And as for your mother — if her heart is set on marrying — let her go back to her powerful father's house. They'll arrange the wedding there and provide the gifts a beloved daughter should have. And here is my own clear advice for you: get the best ship you can, man it with twenty oarsmen, and go searching for your father, gone so long. Someone may tell you something, or you may catch a word from Zeus, the kind that so often carries word to men. First go to Pylos and ask noble Nestor, then on to Sparta to fair-haired Menelaus, last of the bronze-armored Greeks to reach home. If you hear your father's alive and on his way, then hold out one more year, hard as it is. But if you hear he's dead, gone from this world, then come home, heap up a mound for him, give him the full funeral honors he deserves, and hand your mother to a new husband. And once you've seen all that done, search your mind and heart for a way to kill these suitors in your halls — by cunning or in the open. You're too old now to act like a child. Haven't you heard how the whole world praises Orestes for the glory he won, killing Aigisthos, the sly murderer of his famous father? You too, my friend — and I can see how tall and handsome you are — be brave, so that men in years to come will speak well of you. But now I must go down to my fast ship and my crew, who are surely fretting at the wait. Look to this yourself, and remember what I've told you."

Then thoughtful Telemachus answered her: "Stranger, you've spoken to me as kindly as a father to his son, and I will never forget your words. But stay a little longer, eager as you are to be off. Bathe first, ease your heart, and then go back to your ship glad at heart, carrying a gift from me — something fine and precious, a keepsake to treasure, the kind of thing dear friends give one another."

Then grey-eyed Athena answered him: "Don't hold me back now — I'm anxious to be on my way. As for the gift your heart moves you to give me, save it for when I come again, to carry home. Choose a truly fine one, and you'll get its worth in return."

And with that grey-eyed Athena was gone, soaring up and away like a bird — but she had set strength and courage in his heart and made him think of his father more than ever. He turned it over in his mind and was struck with wonder, for he sensed she had been a god. Then, godlike as he was, he went straight back to the suitors.

The famous singer was still singing to them, and they sat in silence, listening, as he told the song of the Greeks' bitter homecoming from Troy, the doom grey-eyed Athena had laid on them. And up in her room, wise Penelope, daughter of Ikarios, heard his haunting song. She came down the high stairs of her house — not alone; two serving women went with her. And when that radiant woman reached the suitors, she stood by the doorpost of the great roofed hall, holding a shimmering veil before her face, a faithful maid on either side. And she wept, and spoke to the god-touched singer:

"Phemios, you know so many other songs that hold men spellbound — the deeds of gods and heroes that singers love to praise. Sing them one of those, and let them drink their wine in silence. But stop this one, this bitter song — every time, it breaks the heart in my breast, because grief beyond all bearing has fallen on me. I long without end for that man, always remembering him — a head whose fame fills all of Greece and the heart of Argos."

Then thoughtful Telemachus answered her: "Mother, why begrudge the loyal singer for lifting our hearts however his spirit moves him? Singers aren't to blame — Zeus is the one to blame, who hands out fortune to working men however he pleases. There's nothing wrong in this man singing the hard fate of the Greeks. People always praise most warmly the newest song that reaches their ears. Steel your heart and listen. Odysseus wasn't the only one who lost the day of his return at Troy; many another good man went down as well. Now go back inside and see to your own work — the loom, the distaff — and tell your women to get on with theirs. Speech will be the men's concern, and mine above all, for the power in this house is mine."

She went back into the house, amazed, and took her son's strong words to heart. Climbing the stairs with her serving women to her room, she wept there for Odysseus, her beloved husband, until grey-eyed Athena cast sweet sleep over her eyes. Down below, the suitors broke into uproar through the shadowy halls, every man praying to lie in her bed.

Then thoughtful Telemachus rounded on them: "Suitors of my mother — you arrogant, overbearing men — let's enjoy the feast for now, and no more shouting. It's a fine thing to listen to a singer like this, with a voice that sounds like a god's. But in the morning let's all take our seats in assembly, so I can give you plain notice to clear out of this house. Feast somewhere else — go through your own provisions, taking turns from house to house. But if you think it's better, easier, to keep grinding down one man's living and pay nothing, then strip it bare. I'll cry out to the everlasting gods, and pray that Zeus pays you back for what you've done. Then you'll die inside these very halls, with no one left to avenge you."

So he spoke, and they all bit their lips, stunned that Telemachus would dare to speak so boldly. Then Antinoos, son of Eupeithes, answered him: "Telemachus, the gods themselves must be teaching you this — to talk big and speak with such nerve. May the son of Kronos never make you king of sea-girt Ithaca, though it's yours by birth, from your father."

And thoughtful Telemachus answered him: "Antinoos, you may not like what I'm about to say, but I'd gladly take that title too, if Zeus would grant it. Do you think being king is the worst thing that could happen to a man? It's no bad thing at all — your house grows rich and you yourself are honored. But there are plenty of other Greek lords in sea-girt Ithaca, young and old, and any one of them might take that throne now that brilliant Odysseus is dead. Even so, I will be master of my own house, and lord over the slaves that godlike Odysseus won for me."

Then Eurymachos, son of Polybos, answered him: "Telemachus, which of us is to be king over the people of Ithaca lies on the knees of the gods. But you will surely keep your own possessions and rule your own house — and may no man ever come to drive you out by force and rob you, not while there's a single soul living in Ithaca. But tell me, my good fellow, about this stranger. Where does the man come from? What land does he claim, what people, what family? Where are his fathers' fields? Did he bring word of your father on his way home, or did he come here on some business of his own? He sprang up and was gone so suddenly, never waiting to be known. And yet, to look at him, he was no low-born man."

And thoughtful Telemachus answered him: "Eurymachos, the day of my father's return is gone for good. I'll never trust another rumor, wherever it comes from, and I pay no attention to the prophecies my mother drags out of some seer she's summoned into the house. As for the stranger — he was a guest-friend of my father's from Taphos. He said he was Mentes, son of wise Anchialos, and that he rules the Taphians, who love their oars." So he spoke — but in his heart he knew it had been an immortal goddess.

Then the suitors turned back to their dancing and the joy of song, and made merry, waiting for evening to come on. And while they were still enjoying themselves, dark night came down — and they went home, each to his own house, to sleep. Telemachus climbed to his own bedroom, built high in the beautiful court, with a clear view all around — and he went up to bed, his mind churning with thoughts. Loyal Eurykleia walked ahead of him, carrying two blazing torches — Eurykleia, daughter of Ops, son of Peisenor. Laertes had bought her, long ago, with his own wealth, when she was just a girl, paying the price of twenty oxen for her. He honored her in his house as much as his own faithful wife, but he never took her to his bed, fearing his wife's anger. She it was who carried the torches for him now, for she loved him more than any of the other serving women, and she had nursed him when he was small. He opened the door of his strongly built room, sat down on the bed, pulled off his soft tunic, and handed it to the wise old woman. She folded it and smoothed it and hung it on a peg beside the corded bedstead, then went out, pulling the door shut by its silver handle and sliding the bolt home with the strap. And there, all night long, wrapped in a fleece of wool, Telemachus lay turning over in his mind the journey grey-eyed Athena had set before him.

books.label: Book II
paragraphs: When the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn, appeared, Telemachus rose from his bed and dressed. He bound the fine sandals on his feet, slung his sword across his shoulder, and walked out of his room looking like a god. At once he sent the heralds out with their clear-voiced call, to summon the long-haired Greeks to assembly. They made the call, the men gathered, and when they were all together Telemachus went to the meeting place, spear in hand — not alone, for two swift hounds went trotting at his heels. And Athena poured such grace over him that the whole crowd marveled as he passed; and when he took his seat, his father's seat, even the grey old elders drew back and made room.

Aigyptios spoke first — a man bent double with age, who had seen everything in his long life. One of his sons, Antiphos, had sailed with Odysseus to Troy, the land of fine horses, and the savage Cyclops had killed him in the cave, made his last grim meal of him. He had three sons still living: two who worked the family land, and a third, Eurynomos, who was one of the suitors. But the father never got over Antiphos, and he was weeping for him still as he began to speak.

"Men of Ithaca, hear me. Not once since the day Odysseus sailed away in his hollow ships have we held a council or an assembly. So who has called us together now? What young man, or what old one, felt the need so badly? Has someone caught word of an army marching on us, and wants to give us warning? Or is there some other public matter to lay before us? Whoever he is, I think him a good man, and I hope Zeus grants him whatever his heart desires."

Telemachus took the old man's words for a good sign, and could sit still no longer — he was bursting to speak. He rose in the middle of the gathering, and the herald Peisenor, a wise man, put the speaker's staff into his hand. Then he turned to Aigyptios first: "Old sir, that man is not far off — you'll soon see for yourself. It was I who called you here, for the grief that falls hardest falls on me. I've caught no word of any army marching on us, nothing to warn you of, and I have no public business to lay before the council. My trouble is my own — two evils that have come down on my house. The first is that I have lost my noble father, who was once king over all of you here, and who was gentle to every one of you, like a father. The second is worse, and it is fast ruining everything I have. The sons of the leading men among you are courting my mother against her will — and they won't go the honest way, to her father Ikarios, and let him weigh the matter, set the bride-price, and give his daughter to the man he favors. No: day after day they camp in my house, slaughtering my oxen and sheep and fat goats, feasting, swilling down my bright wine with never a thought for the cost. There is no fortune on earth that can stand it. We have no Odysseus now to drive this ruin from our doors, and I am not the man to do it myself. I'll never be his equal, hard as I might try — but I would defend myself if I had the strength, for what is being done here is past all bearing. My house is being shamed, eaten down to nothing.

"Be ashamed before your own neighbors, then; be ashamed before the people who live around us. And fear the anger of the gods, lest they turn in fury at these wrongs. I beg you, by Zeus and by Themis, who breaks up the assemblies of men and calls them to order — hold back, my friends, and leave me to my grief alone! Unless, that is, my brave father Odysseus once did some harm to the Greeks, and you are paying it back on me, by setting these men on. As for me — I'd rather you devoured my stores and my cattle yourselves. If you ate them, there might one day be a reckoning: I'd go through the town pressing my claim, demanding payment, until I got back everything I'd lost. But as it stands, there is no remedy, and you have heaped grief on me past all cure."

So he spoke, in a rush of anger, and he dashed the staff to the ground and burst into tears. Pity ran through the whole assembly. The others all sat silent — not one had the heart to answer Telemachus with a hard word — all but Antinoos, who spoke out: "Telemachus, you young hothead, what a speech! Trying to shame us, to pin the blame on us! It is not the suitors who are at fault — it's your own mother, who is cunning beyond all women. Three years now, and the fourth wearing on, she has been leading us by the nose. She gives every one of us hope, sends each man messages and promises — and means not a word of any of it. Her heart is set on something else entirely.

"And here's the trick she played on us. She set up a great loom in her hall and began to weave — a fine, wide web, enormous work — and she said to us: 'Young men, my suitors, since noble Odysseus is dead, you are eager for the wedding, I know; but wait, be patient, until I finish this cloth — I don't want all my spinning to go to waste — a shroud for the hero Laertes, against the day that death's long grief comes and takes him. The women of Ithaca would never forgive me if a man who won so much should lie in his grave without a shroud.' That is what she said, and our proud hearts gave way. So by day she would weave at the great web, and every night, by torchlight, she would unravel what she'd done. For three years the trick held, and we never saw through it. But when the fourth year came around with the turning seasons, one of her women — a girl who knew the whole of it — told us, and we caught her in the act of pulling apart that gleaming cloth. So she had to finish it, whether she wanted to or not.

"So here is the suitors' answer to you — and hear it plainly, you and all the Greeks: send your mother away, and make her marry whichever man her father picks, and she agrees to. But if she means to go on grinding down the sons of the Greeks much longer, trading on the gifts Athena gave her — her rare skill, her cleverness, her scheming mind, the like of which we have never heard, not even in the famous women of the old days, in Tyro or Alkmene or fair-crowned Mykene, none of whom had a mind to match Penelope's — well, this once her scheming will not serve her. As long as she keeps the mind the gods have put in her now, just so long will we keep eating down your house and your living. She wins herself great fame by it; you are the one who pays. And we will not go back to our own lands, here or anywhere else, until she chooses one of us and marries him."

And thoughtful Telemachus answered him: "Antinoos, how can I drive the mother who bore me, who raised me, out of this house, against her will? My father is far away — alive or dead, I do not know. And it would go hard with me to pay back Ikarios the great bride-price I'd owe him if I sent his daughter home of my own accord. Her father would deal harshly with me, and the gods would deal worse — for my mother, leaving this house, would call down the Furies on me. The world would turn against me. No — I will never give that order. If your own consciences are stung by this, then leave my house. Feast somewhere else, work through your own provisions, taking turns from house to house. But if you'd sooner keep grinding down one man's living and pay nothing for it — then strip it bare. I will cry out to the everlasting gods, and pray that Zeus pays you back for what you've done. Then you'll die inside these very halls, and no one left to avenge you."

So spoke Telemachus, and Zeus who sees far sent down two eagles, flying from a high mountain peak. For a while they rode the wind, gliding wing to wing, holding their lordly course. But when they came right over the loud assembly, they wheeled, beating their thick wings, and looked down on the heads of the men below with death in their eyes. Then they tore at each other with their talons — clawing each other's cheeks and necks — and swept off to the right, over the houses of the town. The men stared in wonder at the birds, and asked one another what it could mean. And the old hero Halitherses, son of Mastor, spoke among them — for no man of his time came close to him at reading birds and telling the things that fate had fixed. With good will he spoke out, and said:

"Hear me now, men of Ithaca — and I speak above all to the suitors, for it is on them this disaster rolls. Odysseus will not be far from his own people much longer. Even now he is close, sowing death and doom for these men — and not for them alone; many another of us who live in Ithaca will suffer for it. So let us think, while there's still time, how to put a stop to all this — or let the suitors stop it themselves, which would be far better for them. I am no untried prophet; I know what I am saying. Everything I foretold for that man has come to pass — when the Greeks set sail for Troy, and crafty Odysseus with them, I said he would suffer terribly, lose every one of his companions, and come home in the twentieth year, unknown to all. And now, look — it is all coming true."

Then Eurymachos, son of Polybos, rounded on him: "Off home with you, old man, and prophesy to your own children — or it may go badly for them. When it comes to omens, I can read them far better than you. Plenty of birds wheel about under the sun, and most of them mean nothing at all. Odysseus is dead, far away — and I only wish you had died with him, instead of standing here croaking out your prophecies and stoking the boy's anger, which burns hot enough already. No doubt you're hoping he'll hand you some gift for your household. Well, I'll tell you, and it will come to pass: if you, an old man who ought to know better, talk this young one into something rash, the first to suffer for it will be Telemachus himself — he'll get nothing out of it, with all of us against him. And on you, old man, we'll lay a fine so heavy you'll groan to pay it; the loss will sit hard on you. As for Telemachus, here in front of you all, this is my counsel to him: tell your mother to go back to her father's house. They'll make the wedding there and lay out all the gifts a beloved daughter deserves. Before that, I do not think the sons of the Greeks will give up their wearisome suit — for we fear no one, least of all Telemachus, however long his speeches run, and we care nothing for your fortune-telling, old man. It comes to nothing and only makes us hate you more. We'll go on devouring his living, and pay back not a thing, so long as Penelope keeps the Greeks dangling over this marriage. Day after day we wait, contending for a prize so rare, and never go courting the other women each of us might fittingly wed."

Then thoughtful Telemachus answered him: "Eurymachos — and the rest of you proud suitors — I'll plead with you no more; I have said all I have to say. The gods know how things stand now, and so do all the Greeks. Give me one thing only: a fast ship and a crew of twenty men, to carry me there and back. I'm going to Sparta and to sandy Pylos, to ask after my father, gone so long. Someone may tell me something, or I may catch a word from Zeus, the kind that so often carries news to men. If I hear my father is alive and on his way home, then I'll hold out one more year, hard as it is. But if I hear he is dead, gone from this world, then I'll come home, heap up a mound for him, give him the full funeral honors he deserves, and hand my mother to a new husband."

With that he sat down. Then Mentor rose to speak — an old friend of faultless Odysseus, the man to whom Odysseus, sailing away, had handed his whole household, charging them all to obey the old man and keep everything safe. With good will he spoke out among them: "Hear me now, men of Ithaca. I hope no sceptered king is ever again kind, or gentle, or fair-minded — I hope every one of them, from now on, is cruel and crooked in his dealings. For not a single man here remembers godlike Odysseus, who ruled over you and was as gentle as a father. I do not blame the suitors so much, for their violence at least is out in the open: they are gambling with their own heads, betting that Odysseus will never come back, and so they eat up his house by force. It is the rest of you I cannot stomach — sitting there in silence, never once speaking out to stop them, when you are many and they are few."

Then Leokritos, son of Euenor, answered him: "Mentor, you reckless fool, what are you saying — setting the people on us to hold us back? It is a hard fight, against odds like these, to come between men and their dinner. Why, even if Odysseus of Ithaca came home himself and found us proud suitors feasting in his hall, and his heart burned to drive us out of it — even so his wife, for all her longing to see him, would take no joy in his return: he'd meet an ugly death there, taking on so many men at once. You're talking nonsense. Come now — break this up. Everyone back to his own work. And let Mentor and Halitherses, old friends of his father, speed this boy on his journey — if he goes at all. But my guess is he'll sit right here in Ithaca, waiting for news to come to him, and never make the voyage."
On that he broke up the assembly, and the people scattered, each to his own house, while the suitors went back to the house of godlike Odysseus.

But Telemachus walked off alone, down to the shore. He washed his hands in the grey seawater and prayed to Athena: "Hear me, you god who came to my house yesterday and told me to take a ship across the misty sea and search out word of my father, gone so long. I want to obey — but the Greeks are blocking my way, and the suitors most of all, in their cruelty and pride."

So he prayed, and Athena came up close, taking the shape and the voice of Mentor, and her words flew straight to him: "Telemachus, you'll be no fool and no coward from this day on, if even a little of your father's spirit runs in you — and what a man he was at finishing what he set out to do. This voyage of yours will not come to nothing. But if you were not truly his son, born of Penelope, then I'd have no hope you would ever bring it off. Few sons turn out the equals of their fathers; most fall short, and only a handful surpass them. But since you'll be neither fool nor coward from now on, and Odysseus' own wisdom is not lost in you, I have good hope you'll see this through. So put the suitors and their scheming out of your mind — there is no sense or justice in them, and they cannot see the death and the dark fate standing close, ready to fall on them all in a single day. The voyage you long for will not be long delayed. I was such a friend to your father that I myself will find you a fast ship and sail with you. Go home now, and move among the suitors. Make your stores ready, pack everything in good vessels — the wine in jars, the barley meal, the marrow of men's strength, in stout leather bags. I'll go through the town and gather a willing crew. There are many ships in sea-girt Ithaca, old and new; I'll look them over and choose you the best. We'll fit her out fast and put to sea."

So spoke Athena, daughter of Zeus, and Telemachus did not linger once he had heard the goddess. He went home with a heavy heart and found the proud suitors there in his courtyard, skinning goats and singeing pigs over the fire. Antinoos came straight up to him, laughing, and caught his hand in his own: "Telemachus, you fiery young speechmaker — let it go, all of it, the hard words and the hard feelings. Eat and drink with us, the way you used to. The Greeks will see to everything for you — a ship and a picked crew — so you can sail to holy Pylos and get news of your noble father."

And thoughtful Telemachus drew his hand away and answered: "Antinoos, there is no eating in peace with men like you, no taking any pleasure in it. Wasn't it enough that you wasted so much of what was mine, all the good things, while I was still a boy? Now I am grown, and I've learned the truth by listening to others, and the spirit has risen in me. I'll loose every ruin I can on you — whether I go to Pylos or stay right here among my own people. I am going, and the voyage I speak of will not be in vain — though I go as a passenger, with no ship and no crew of my own, since that is how you suitors thought best to leave me."

So he spoke, and snatched his hand from Antinoos' grip. All through the house the suitors went on with their feast, and they mocked him as they worked, throwing taunts. One brash young man would say: "There's no doubt Telemachus is plotting our murder. He'll bring back fighting men from sandy Pylos, or from Sparta — he's set his heart on it. Or maybe he means to sail to Ephyra, that rich land, and come home with deadly poison to drop in the wine-bowl and finish us all." And another would say: "Who knows — once he's off on his hollow ship, he may wander far from his friends and die, just like his father. Then we'd have all the more to do, splitting his goods among us — though we'd leave the house itself to his mother and the man who marries her."

So they talked. But Telemachus went down to his father's storeroom, a high, broad chamber where gold and bronze lay heaped, and chests of clothing, and a great store of fragrant olive oil. There stood jars of old wine, sweet and unmixed, a drink fit for a god, ranged in order along the wall, waiting for the day long-suffering Odysseus might come home at last. The room was shut with close-fitted double doors, and watch over it, night and day, was kept by the housekeeper Eurykleia, daughter of Ops, son of Peisenor — careful and wise in all things. Telemachus called her into the storeroom and said: "Nurse, draw me off some wine in jars — sweet wine, the best after the vintage you're keeping for my poor father, in case that man, escaping death and doom, ever comes home. Fill me twelve jars and seal them all with lids. And pour out barley meal into stitched leather bags — twenty measures of ground grain. Tell no one. Have it all put together; I'll come for it this evening, once my mother has gone up to her room to sleep. I am going to Sparta and to sandy Pylos, to see what I can learn of my dear father's return."

When she heard him, the dear old nurse Eurykleia cried out, and the tears came, and she spoke from the heart: "Dear child, how could such a thing get into your head? Where would you go, across the whole wide world — you, an only son, and so beloved? Noble Odysseus is dead and gone, far from his country, somewhere among strangers. And the moment your back is turned, these men will be plotting against you, scheming to kill you by a trick and split everything you own among themselves. Stay here, with what is yours. There is no need for you to suffer, wandering over the barren sea."

And thoughtful Telemachus answered her: "Take heart, nurse — there's a god behind this plan. But swear to me you'll say nothing of it to my mother until eleven or twelve days have passed, or until she misses me herself and hears that I've gone. I don't want her spoiling her lovely face with tears." So he spoke, and the old woman swore a great oath by the gods to keep silent. And when she had sworn it and the oath was done, she drew off the wine into the jars and poured the barley meal into the stout leather bags, while Telemachus went back inside to the suitors.

Then grey-eyed Athena thought of the next thing. Taking the form of Telemachus, she ranged through the town, going up to each man of the crew and telling them to gather at the fast ship by nightfall. And she asked Noemon, the fine son of Phronios, for a swift ship, and he gave it gladly. The sun went down and the streets grew dark. She hauled the ship to the water, stowed in her all the gear that well-benched ships carry, and brought her to rest at the harbor's mouth. The good crew gathered around, and the goddess heartened every man.

Then grey-eyed Athena thought of one more thing. She went to the house of godlike Odysseus and poured sweet sleep over the suitors, fuddling them as they drank, knocking the cups from their hands. They could sit no longer over their wine; they shuffled off into the town to find their beds, their eyes already heavy with sleep. Then Athena, in the shape and voice of Mentor, called Telemachus out of his hall: "Telemachus, your men are aboard and at the oars, waiting for the word from you. Come, let's not put off the voyage."

With that, Pallas Athena led the way, swiftly, and Telemachus followed in the god's footsteps. When they came down to the ship and the sea, they found the long-haired crew waiting on the shore, and Telemachus, in his strength, said to them: "This way, friends — let's bring the stores aboard. They're all set out together in the hall. My mother knows nothing of it, nor do the serving women — only one of them." So he spoke, and led the way, and they came after. They carried it all down and stowed it in the well-benched ship, just as Odysseus' dear son directed. Then Telemachus stepped aboard, with Athena going before him, and she took her seat in the stern, and he sat down beside her. The men loosed the cables, climbed aboard, and settled at the oars. And grey-eyed Athena sent them a fair wind, a fresh West Wind singing over the wine-dark sea. Telemachus called out to the crew to lay hold of the rigging, and they obeyed. They raised the fir mast, stepped it in its hollow socket, and made it fast with the forestays; then they hauled up the white sail with twisted oxhide ropes. The wind bellied out the sail, and the dark wave roared loud about the stem as the ship ran on, racing over the swell, holding her course. They made the tackle fast all through the swift black ship, and then they set out mixing-bowls brimful of wine and poured offerings to the deathless gods who live forever — but above all to the grey-eyed daughter of Zeus. And so, all night long and into the dawn, the ship cut on through the sea.
books.title: Telemachus Calls the Assembly

books.label: Book III
paragraphs: As the sun climbed out of the lovely sea into the bronze sky, to bring its light to gods and mortals alike, they came to Pylos, the well-built city of Neleus. The people were down on the shore, sacrificing jet-black bulls to Poseidon, the dark-maned shaker of the earth. There were nine companies seated there, five hundred men in each, and each had brought nine bulls to offer. They were tasting the inner meats and burning the thigh-bones to the god just as Telemachus and his crew sailed in. The men furled the sails, brought the ship to anchor, and stepped ashore.

Athena led the way, and Telemachus came after her. Then she said to him: "Telemachus, there's no place for shyness now, not even a little. You crossed the sea for this — to learn where your father lies and how he met his end. So go straight up to Nestor. Let's see what he can tell us. Ask him to speak the truth, and he will — he's far too good a man to lie."

"But how, Mentor?" Telemachus answered. "How do I walk up to a man like that, and what do I even say? I've never been one for long speeches with anyone, and I'm ashamed to start by questioning a man so much older than I am."

Then grey-eyed Athena said: "Some of it, Telemachus, your own heart will tell you what to say, and the rest a god will put into your mind. I'm sure of it — the gods have been with you from the day you were born until now."

She went on quickly, and Telemachus followed in her steps until they reached the place where the men of Pylos were gathered. There sat Nestor with his sons, and all around them his people were busy with the feast — roasting some meat on the spits, threading more onto them. The moment they saw the strangers, the men crowded forward, clasped their hands in welcome, and waved them to seats. Nestor's son Pisistratus reached them first; he took each by the hand and settled them on soft fleeces spread over the sand, beside his father and his brother Thrasymedes. Then he handed them their share of the inner meats and poured them wine in a golden cup, lifting it first to Athena, and he greeted her as he gave it:

"Stranger, say a prayer to Lord Poseidon — it's his feast you've come to share. When you've prayed and made your offering, pass the cup to your friend so he can pour his too. He prays as well, I'm sure, for no man can live without the gods. But he's the younger of you, near my own age, so I'll give you the cup first."

With that he put the golden cup in her hand. Athena was pleased — it was right and fitting of him to give it first to her — and she began to pray in earnest to Poseidon: "Hear me, Poseidon, holder of the earth, and don't grudge us, for all our praying, the fulfilling of what we've come to do. First grant glory to Nestor and his sons, and then send the people of Pylos a fair return for this great offering. And last, grant Telemachus and me a safe passage and a good end to the errand that brought our swift ship here."

So she prayed — and made it all come true herself. Then she handed the lovely cup to Telemachus, and Odysseus' dear son prayed in his turn. When the outer meats were roasted and drawn off the spits, they cut everyone his portion and feasted well. And when they had all had their fill of food and drink, Nestor, the old knight of Gerene, began to speak.

"Now that our guests have eaten," he said, "it's a fair time to ask who they are. Tell us, then, strangers — who are you, and from what harbor have you sailed? Are you traders on some business? Or do you roam the sea like raiders, who risk their lives to bring ruin to other men?"

Telemachus answered him boldly now, for Athena herself had put courage in his heart to ask about his lost father and so win himself a name. "Nestor, son of Neleus, great glory of the Greeks — you ask where we come from, and I'll tell you. We come from Ithaca, below Mount Neion, and my errand is my own, not the people's. I'm searching for word of my father, long-suffering Odysseus, who they say once sacked the city of Troy at your side. We know what fate found every other man who fought there — but of Odysseus the gods have hidden even the manner of his death. No one can tell us where he died: whether he fell on dry land, cut down by enemies, or was lost at sea in the waves.
