But the moment your hands touch land, untie it and fling it far out into the wine-dark sea, well clear of the shore, and turn your face away." With that the goddess gave him the veil, and dove back down into the heaving sea like a gull, and the dark water closed over her.

But long-suffering, brilliant Odysseus was torn, and groaned to his own great spirit: "No — I'm afraid this is one of the immortals weaving me another trap, telling me to leave my raft. I won't do it, not yet. That land where she says I'll be safe — I saw with my own eyes it's still a long way off. Here's what I'll do, and I think it's best: as long as the timbers hold together, I'll stay aboard and ride out the worst. But the moment the sea smashes the raft to pieces, then I'll swim for it — there's nothing better I can think of than that."

While he was still turning it over in his mind, Poseidon the earth-shaker raised up a great wave, terrible and crushing, towering over him, and brought it down. As a wild gust scatters a dry heap of chaff and flings it every way, so the long timbers flew apart. Odysseus threw himself astride a single beam and rode it like a man on horseback, and stripped off the clothes Calypso had given him, and wound Ino's veil beneath his chest, and plunged headlong into the sea, his arms spread to swim. And lord Poseidon, the shaker of the earth, saw him do it, and shook his head, and muttered to his own heart: "There — now drift in misery across the sea, until you fall in with men whom the gods have favored. Even so, I don't think you'll find your suffering too light." With that he whipped his fine-maned horses on and drove to Aegae, where his glorious palace stands.

But Athena, daughter of Zeus, had other plans. She bound back the paths of all the other winds and ordered them to rest, to fall still and sleep — all but the swift North Wind, which she roused, and she broke the waves down ahead of brilliant Odysseus, so that he might reach the Phaeacians, who love their oars, and slip past death and doom.

For two nights then, and two days, he drifted on the heavy swell, and again and again his heart looked his own death in the face. But when fair-haired Dawn brought on the third day, the wind died and a windless calm came over the sea, and there, as he was lifted high on a great swell and peered ahead with straining eyes, he saw land close by. As welcome as the first sign of life is to children, when their father lies sick, racked with long agony, wasting under some cruel god's hand, and then the gods set him free of the evil — that welcome was the sight of land and trees to Odysseus, and he swam hard for it, longing to set his feet on solid ground. But when he had come within shouting distance of the shore, he heard the boom of the surf against the rocks. Great waves were thundering in against the dry land with a terrible roar, and everything was sheeted in spray. There were no harbors there to hold a ship, no roadstead — only headlands jutting out, and reefs, and cliffs.

And the knees of Odysseus went slack, and his heart with them, and he groaned to his own great spirit: "What now? Zeus has let me see the land I'd given up all hope of, and I've cut my way clear across this gulf — but there's no way out of the gray water, no foothold. Sharp rocks ahead, and the surf roaring all around them, and the cliff rising up sheer and smooth, with deep water hard against it, no place to stand on my two feet and pull free of this ruin. If I try to climb out, a great wave will lift me and dash me against the jagged rock, and my struggle is for nothing. But if I swim on further, looking for a beach that shelves easy, or a quiet harbor, I'm afraid the storm will snatch me up again, groaning, and carry me back out over the teeming sea — or some god will send a great monster up against me from the deep, the kind that famed Amphitrite breeds by the thousand. For I know how the great earth-shaker hates me."

While he was still turning it over in his mind, a great wave carried him in against the rugged shore. There he would have been flayed, his bones broken, had not grey-eyed Athena put it into his heart what to do. He lunged with both hands and caught the rock and clung to it, groaning, until the great wave had passed. So he rode that one out — but then the backwash struck him and flung him far out to sea again. As when an octopus is torn from its hole and the pebbles cling thick to its suckers, so the skin was stripped from his strong hands against the rock, and the great wave closed over him. And there, against all his fate, poor Odysseus would have died, had not grey-eyed Athena given him a clear head. He fought up clear of the surf where it pounded the shore, and swam along outside it, his eyes always on the land, looking for a beach that shelved easy or a harbor out of the sea's reach. And as he swam he came to the mouth of a fair-running river, and that, he saw, was the best place of all — smooth, no rocks, and sheltered from the wind. He felt the river's current running and he prayed to it in his heart:

"Hear me, lord, whoever you are. I come to you as the answer to all my prayers, fleeing the sea and Poseidon's threats. Even the deathless gods honor the man who comes to them lost and wandering, the way I come now to your stream and your knees, after so much suffering. Take pity on me, lord. I am your suppliant, and I claim it."

So he prayed, and the river-god at once held back his current and stilled the waves, and made the water smooth before him, and brought him safe to land at the river's mouth. There at last his knees gave way, and his strong hands, for the sea had broken him utterly. His whole body was swollen, and the sea-water ran streaming from his mouth and nose, and he lay there with no breath in him and no voice, worn out past all enduring. But when at last he caught his breath and the spirit gathered again in his heart, he untied the goddess's veil from his body and let it fall into the seaward-running river, and a great wave bore it back down the current, and Ino caught it in her hands at once. Then he turned from the river, sank down in the reeds, and kissed the grain-giving earth.

And still, in his misery, he groaned to his own great spirit: "What now — what's to become of me, here at the end of everything? If I keep watch by the river through the long, anxious night, the bitter frost and the soaking dew may finish me off, weak as I am, breath barely in me — and a cold wind blows up off a river toward dawn. But if I climb the slope to the shadowy woods and lie down to sleep in the thick brush, even if the cold and the weariness let me be and sweet sleep comes — I'm afraid I'll be left as prey, a meal for the wild beasts."

In the end this seemed the better course. He went up toward the woods and found a thicket on rising ground, in a clearing near the water. There he crept in under two olive trees grown from a single root — one a wild olive, the other a cultivated one. No force of the wet, blustering wind could reach through them, no ray of the blazing sun, no soaking rain, so closely had they grown into each other. Odysseus crept in under them, and at once he raked together a wide bed for himself, for there was a great drift of fallen leaves there, enough to cover two men, or three, in the hard weather of deep winter. Brilliant, long-suffering Odysseus saw it and was glad, and lay down in the middle and heaped the fallen leaves over himself. As a man on a lonely farm, far from any neighbor, will bury a glowing brand in the black ashes to save the seed of fire, so he would not have to go begging a light from somewhere else — so Odysseus buried himself in the leaves. And Athena poured sleep over his eyes, and closed his lids, to release him as quickly as she could from his bone-deep weariness.

[Trans. note: The veil Ino gives him is her krēdemnon — a woman's head-binding worn over the hair and drawn across the face. Older versions render it "scarf" or "veil"; we keep "veil," the closest plain English, but the thing is a headdress, an intimate gift of her own covering, immortal and protecting.]
books.title: Calypso, and the Raft

books.label: Book VI
paragraphs: So long-suffering, brilliant Odysseus slept there, worn down by sleep and toil. But Athena went off to the country and the city of the Phaeacians. These people had once lived in the broad land of Hypereia, hard by the Cyclopes, a lawless and overbearing race who were stronger than they were and forever raiding them. So their king, godlike Nausithous, moved them away and settled them in Scheria, far from all other men who live by their labor. He ringed the city with a wall, built houses and temples for the gods, and parceled out the fields. But by now he had gone down, beaten by his fate, to the house of Hades, and Alcinous ruled in his place, a man whose counsels the gods themselves had taught him. It was to his house that grey-eyed Athena came, turning over in her mind the homecoming of great-hearted Odysseus.

She went straight to the richly worked bedchamber where a girl was sleeping who had the form and face of a goddess — Nausicaa, the daughter of great-hearted Alcinous. Two handmaids, lovely as the Graces, lay one on either side of the door, and the gleaming doors were shut. Athena drifted to the girl's bedside like a breath of wind. She had taken the shape of the daughter of Dymas, a famous seafaring man — a girl Nausicaa's own age, and dear to her heart. In that likeness grey-eyed Athena spoke:

"Nausicaa, how did your mother come to have so careless a daughter? Your bright clothes are lying about, neglected — and your wedding is near, when you'll need fine things to wear yourself and fine things to give the bridal party who walk beside you. This is how a girl earns a good name among people, and how she makes her father and her lady mother proud. So come, let's go and wash at the first light of dawn. I'll go along to help, so the work goes quickly, for you won't be a maiden much longer. Already the best young men of all the Phaeacians, your own people, are courting you. Go at first light and ask your noble father to make ready the mules and the cart, to carry the sashes and the robes and the bright bedding. It's better for you to ride than to go on foot — the washing-pools are a long way from the town."

With that, grey-eyed Athena went away to Olympus, where they say the gods have their seat forever, unshaken. No wind shakes it, no rain ever wets it, no snow comes near; the air spreads cloudless and clear, and a white radiance plays over it. There the blessed gods take their pleasure, all their days. To that place the grey-eyed one went, when she had finished with the girl.

Soon Dawn came to her lovely throne and woke Nausicaa of the fine robes. She marveled at her dream, and went off through the house to tell her father and her mother, and she found the two of them inside. Her mother sat at the hearth with her serving women, spinning yarn dyed with sea-purple. She caught her father at the door, on his way out to join the lords of the Phaeacians at their council, where the noblest men had summoned him. She came up close and said:

"Papa, dear — won't you have them harness me a high cart with good wheels, so I can take our fine clothes down to the river to wash? They're lying soiled. And it's right that you yourself should wear clean things when you sit in council among the leading men. And there are five sons of yours under this roof — two of them married, three still in the flower of youth and unwed, and they always want fresh-washed clothes for the dance. All of this is on my mind to see to."

So she spoke, for she was shy of naming her own ripe marriage to her dear father. But he understood it all, and answered her: "I'll not grudge you the mules, child, nor anything else. Off you go — the men will harness you a high cart with good wheels, fitted with a body to hold it all."

With that he called to the servants, and they obeyed. They wheeled the cart out, smooth-running, and harnessed the mules to it and yoked them in, while the girl carried the bright clothes down from her room and stacked them in the polished cart. Her mother packed a hamper with all kinds of good food to eat, and put in savory things, and filled a goatskin with wine; and as the girl climbed up, she gave her soft olive oil in a golden flask, so she and her maids could rub themselves down after the bath. Then Nausicaa took the whip and the bright reins and cracked them to start the mules. They strained against the harness with a clatter of hooves, carrying the clothes and the girl — not alone, for her handmaids walked along beside her.

When they reached the beautiful stream of the river, where the washing-pools never failed — clear water welling up in plenty to wash the dirtiest clothes — they unyoked the mules from the cart and turned them loose along the eddying river to graze on the honey-sweet grass. They lifted the clothes down from the cart by armfuls, carried them into the dark water, and trod them down in the pits, each girl racing the others at the work. When they had washed them and rinsed every stain away, they spread them out in a row along the seashore, where the surf had washed the shingle cleanest. Then they bathed, and rubbed themselves with the glistening oil, and ate their meal beside the banks of the river, and waited for the clothes to dry in the heat of the sun. And when she and her maids had eaten their fill, they threw off their headscarves and played at ball, and Nausicaa of the white arms led their singing. She moved among them like Artemis the archer ranging the mountains — down the long ridge of Taygetus or Erymanthus, delighting in the wild boar and the swift deer, while the wild nymphs, daughters of Zeus who holds the storm-shield, play at the hunt beside her, and Leto's heart lifts to see her own girl standing a head taller than them all, easy to pick out, lovely as they all are. So this unwed girl outshone her women.

But when she was about to fold the fine clothes, yoke the mules, and turn for home, grey-eyed Athena thought of something else — that Odysseus should wake and see the lovely girl, and she should lead him to the city of the Phaeacians. The princess threw the ball to one of her maids; it missed her and dropped into a deep eddy of the river, and they all cried out, loud and clear. And brilliant Odysseus woke. He sat up, and a question turned in his heart and mind:

"What sorrow — whose country have I come to this time? Are they cruel men, savage, with no sense of right? Or do they welcome strangers, and fear the gods in their hearts? That sounded to me like the high cry of girls — like the nymphs who haunt the steep peaks of the mountains, and the springs of rivers, and the grassy water-meadows. Or am I somewhere near people who speak as I do? Let me go and see for myself."

With that, brilliant Odysseus crept out from under the bushes, and with his strong hand he broke off a leafy branch from the thick wood, to hold across his body and cover his nakedness. And out he came, like a lion bred in the hills, sure of its strength, that goes out through wind and rain with its eyes ablaze, and falls on the cattle and the sheep, or hunts the wild deer — its belly drives it to break even into a close-fenced steading after the flock. So Odysseus, in his hard need, made ready to wade in among the girls with their lovely hair, naked as he was. He came toward them, caked with brine, a terrible sight, and they scattered in fear, this way and that, along the jutting spits of the shore. Only the daughter of Alcinous held her ground, for Athena put courage in her heart and took the fear from her limbs. She stood and faced him. And Odysseus turned it over — whether to clasp the lovely girl's knees and beg, or stand off at a distance and plead in gentle words that she give him clothes and show him the way to the town. In the end this seemed the better course: to plead from a distance, in gentle words, for fear that if he took hold of her knees the girl would be angry. So at once he spoke, in words that were honeyed and shrewd:

"I am your suppliant, my lady — but are you a goddess, or a mortal woman? If you are a goddess, one of those who hold the wide heaven, then to my eyes you are most like Artemis, the daughter of great Zeus, in your beauty and your bearing and your height. But if you are mortal, one of those who live on the earth, then three times blessed are your father and your honored mother, and three times blessed your brothers — their hearts must always glow with warmth and joy on your account, when they watch a flower like you step into the dance. But blessed beyond them all, beyond all others, is the man who will load the wedding-gifts and lead you home. For never yet have my eyes seen such a one among mortals, neither man nor woman. Looking at you, I am struck with awe. Once, at Delos, by the altar of Apollo, I saw the like — a young palm tree shooting up; for there I went, too, and a great host of people followed me, on that road that was to be the start of all my troubles. And just as, seeing that, I stood and marveled long in my heart, for no such tree had ever risen from the earth — so I marvel now at you, my lady, and stand in awe, and dare not touch your knees, though my grief is deep. Yesterday, on the twentieth day, I escaped the wine-dark sea; until then the waves and the rushing winds carried me on and on from the island of Ogygia. And now some power has cast me up here, to suffer still more, no doubt — for I don't think my troubles are over yet, but the gods have much in store for me before that.

"So pity me, my lady. After all I have suffered, you are the first I have come to; I know no one else among the people who hold this city and this land. Show me the way to the town, and give me a rag to throw around me — anything you brought to wrap the clothes in. And may the gods grant you all your heart desires: a husband, and a home, and the gift of one mind between you. For there is nothing finer, nothing stronger than this — when two people keep house together, of one heart and one mind, a grief to those who hate them and a joy to those who wish them well; and they themselves know it best of all."

Then Nausicaa of the white arms answered him: "Stranger, you seem to be no fool, and no bad man. It is Olympian Zeus himself who deals out fortune to people, to the good and the bad alike, each man as he pleases — and these troubles are his gift to you, and you must simply bear them. But now that you have reached our city and our land, you shall not go short of clothes, nor of anything else a hard-pressed suppliant has the right to ask of those he meets. I'll show you the way to the town, and tell you the name of our people. We are the Phaeacians who hold this city and this land, and I am the daughter of great-hearted Alcinous, in whom all the strength and power of the Phaeacians rests."

Then she called to her maids with their lovely hair: "Stop where you are, girls. Where are you running, at the sight of a man? You don't think he's an enemy, surely? There is no man living, and there never will be, who could come to the Phaeacians' land bent on harm, for we are very dear to the immortal gods. We live far off, at the edge of the world, in the surging sea, with no other people near us. No — this is some luckless wanderer who has come here, and we must care for him now; for all strangers and beggars come from Zeus, and a small gift, given freely, is dear to them. So give the stranger food and drink, girls, and bathe him in the river where there's shelter from the wind."

At that they stopped, and called out to one another to come back, and they sat Odysseus down in a sheltered spot, as Nausicaa, the daughter of great-hearted Alcinous, had told them. They laid out clothes for him, a tunic and a cloak, and gave him the soft oil in its golden flask, and told him to bathe in the river's stream. But then brilliant Odysseus spoke to the maids: "Stand off a little way, girls, so I can wash the brine from my shoulders myself and rub myself with oil — it's a long time since my skin has felt it. I won't bathe in front of you. I am ashamed to stand naked among girls with such lovely hair."

So he spoke, and they went off and told the girl. And brilliant Odysseus washed the brine from his back and his broad shoulders with the river water, and scrubbed the dried salt from his hair. When he had washed all over and rubbed himself with oil, he put on the clothes the unwed girl had given him. And Athena, the daughter of Zeus, made him look taller and broader to the eye, and made the hair fall thick from his head in curls like the hyacinth flower. As when a master craftsman, schooled by Hephaestus and Athena in every art, washes gold over silver and makes a thing of beauty — so the goddess poured grace over his head and his shoulders. Then he went and sat apart, down along the shore, shining with grace and beauty, and the girl gazed at him. And she said to her maids with their lovely hair:

"Listen to me, my white-armed girls, while I say something. It is not against the will of all the gods who hold Olympus that this man has come among the godlike Phaeacians. A moment ago he seemed to me a wretched thing, and now he looks like the gods who hold the wide heaven. If only a man like that might be called my husband, settled here, and content to stay. But give the stranger food and drink, girls."

So she spoke, and they listened and obeyed, and set food and drink before Odysseus. And long-suffering, brilliant Odysseus ate and drank, ravenous — for it had been a long time since he had tasted food. Then Nausicaa of the white arms thought of something else. She folded the clothes and stowed them in the fine cart, and yoked the strong-hooved mules, and climbed up herself. Then she urged Odysseus on, and spoke to him plainly:

"Up now, stranger, and into the town — I'll bring you as far as my wise father's house, where I promise you'll meet all the noblest of the Phaeacians. Only do as I say; you seem to be a man of sense. As long as we're crossing the fields and the farmlands, walk quickly behind the mules and the cart with the maids, and I'll lead the way. But when we come near the town — there's a high wall around it, and a fine harbor on each side of the city, with a narrow channel in between, and the curved ships are drawn up along the road, for every man has a slip of his own. There's the gathering-place, around the beautiful temple of Poseidon, fitted with great stones bedded deep in the ground. There the people see to the gear of the black ships, the cables and the sails, and there they plane down the oars. For the Phaeacians care nothing for the bow and the quiver, only for masts and oars and the trim ships they take such joy in, crossing the gray sea.

"It's the talk of these people I want to avoid — their cold gossip later on, for there are insolent men among them, and some low fellow might meet us and say: 'Who's this — this tall, handsome stranger trailing after Nausicaa? Where did she pick him up? She'll be making him her husband, no doubt. Some castaway she's taken in off his ship, from far away — for we have no neighbors here — or some god she prayed and prayed for has come down at last from heaven, and she'll have him all her days. Better so, if she's gone and found herself a husband somewhere else; for she looks down on her own people here, the Phaeacians, fine and many as they are, who court her.' That's what they'll say, and it would be a reproach to me. And I'd think the same myself of another girl who did the like — who, with her father and her mother living, went about with men before the day of her open wedding.

"So do as I say, stranger, and you'll soon win your passage home and an escort from my father. You'll find a fine grove of poplars near the road, sacred to Athena, with a spring running through it and a meadow all around. There my father has his estate and his flowering orchard, no farther from the town than a man's shout will carry. Sit down there and wait a while, until we've had time to reach the town and come to my father's house. Then, when you judge we've reached it, go into the city of the Phaeacians yourself, and ask the way to the house of great-hearted Alcinous, my father. It's easy to know — any little child could lead you to it, for the other Phaeacians have no houses built like the hall of the hero Alcinous. But once the house and the courtyard take you in, go quickly across the great hall to my mother. She sits at the hearth in the firelight, leaning against a pillar, spinning sea-purple yarn, a wonder to behold, with her serving women ranged behind her. My father's chair stands close to hers, and there he sits and drinks his wine like an immortal. Pass him by, and throw your arms around my mother's knees, if you want to see the glad day of your homecoming soon, however far away your home may be. If she takes you to her heart, then you may hope to see your own people again, and come back to your high-roofed house and the land of your fathers."

With that she cracked the bright whip over the mules, and they left the streams of the river behind. The mules ran well, working their legs in good rhythm, and she handled the reins with care, so that Odysseus and the maids could keep pace on foot — using the whip with judgment. The sun was going down when they came to the famous grove sacred to Athena, and there brilliant Odysseus sat down. At once he prayed to the daughter of mighty Zeus:

"Hear me, child of Zeus who holds the storm-shield, you who never tire. Hear me now — though you would not hear me before, when the great earth-shaker was breaking me on the sea. Grant that I come to the Phaeacians welcomed, and pitied."

So he prayed, and Pallas Athena heard him. But she would not yet show herself to him face to face, out of respect for her father's brother Poseidon, who still kept up his rage against godlike Odysseus until the day he reached his own land.
books.title: Nausicaa

books.label: Book VII
paragraphs: So Odysseus waited there and prayed, while the girl drove on into the town. When she reached her father's house she pulled up at the gate, and her brothers — handsome as gods — came crowding round her. They loosed the mules from the wagon and carried the clothes inside, and Nausicaa went to her own room, where an old serving woman, Eurymedusa of Apeira, lit the fire for her. Long ago she had been carried over the sea from Apeira and given to Alcinous as a prize of honor, for he was king over the Phaeacians and the people obeyed him as though he were a god. She had been Nausicaa's nurse, and now she kindled the fire and brought the girl her supper in her room.

Then Odysseus rose to go on toward the town, and Athena wrapped a thick mist all around him, so that none of the proud Phaeacians who crossed his path might insult him or ask who he was. And just as he was about to enter the town, she came to meet him in the form of a young girl carrying a pitcher. She stopped right in front of him, and Odysseus said:
"My child, would you be kind enough to show me the house of King Alcinous? I'm a stranger here, down on my luck, and I don't know a soul in your town or your country."

Then grey-eyed Athena answered him: "Of course, good stranger, I'll show you the house you're looking for — it stands close by my own father's. Only come quietly, and don't say a word, and don't look any man in the face or ask him questions. The people here have little patience with strangers and don't take kindly to anyone from somewhere else. They're a seafaring folk, and by the grace of Poseidon they sail the deep in ships swift as a thought, or as a bird on the wing."

With that she led the way, and Odysseus followed in her steps; but not one of the Phaeacians could see him as he passed through their midst, for the great goddess in her care for him had hidden him in a thick cloud of darkness. He marveled at their harbors and their trim ships, at their meeting-places and the high city walls, fitted with palisades — a wonder to look on. And when they reached the king's house, Athena said:

"This is the house, good stranger, that you asked me to show you. You'll find a crowd of great men sitting at table inside, but don't be afraid — go straight in. A bold man comes out ahead in everything, even one who arrives a stranger from far away. The first one you must find is the queen. Her name is Arete, and she comes of the very same line as her husband Alcinous. They both go back to Poseidon, who fathered Nausithous on Periboea, the loveliest of women — the youngest daughter of Eurymedon, who once ruled the reckless Giants, and brought his doomed people to ruin, and was destroyed himself.

"But Poseidon lay with his daughter Periboea, and she bore him a son, great-hearted Nausithous, who reigned over the Phaeacians. Nausithous in turn had two sons, Rhexenor and Alcinous. Apollo struck down the first while he was still a young bridegroom, with no son of his own — but he left a daughter, Arete, and Alcinous made her his wife, and he honors her as no other woman on earth is honored, of all who keep house under a husband's roof.

"From the start she has been cherished with all his heart — by Alcinous himself, by their children, and by the whole people, who look on her as something more than mortal and salute her with their eyes whenever she walks through the city. For there is no better woman, in mind or in heart, and the men whose wives are her friends she helps to settle even their own quarrels. Win her good will, and you have every hope of seeing the ones you love again, and coming home at last to your own high-roofed house and your native land."

With that grey-eyed Athena left Scheria and went out over the barren sea — to Marathon, and the wide streets of Athens, where she passed into the strong house of Erechtheus. But Odysseus came up to the house of Alcinous, and his heart turned over many things as he paused on the bronze threshold before crossing it, for a light shone through the high-roofed house of great-hearted Alcinous like the gleam of the sun or the moon. The walls ran in bronze from the doorway to the inmost room, and the cornice above them was a deep blue enamel. The doors were of gold, hung on silver posts that rose from a floor of bronze; the lintel above was silver, and the door-handle was gold.

On either side of the doorway stood dogs of gold and silver, which Hephaestus had made with all his cunning skill to guard the house of great-hearted Alcinous — deathless, and never to grow old, for all their days. Benches stood ranged along the wall, this side and that, from the threshold to the inmost chamber, spread with finely woven covers that the women of the house had made. Here the leading men of the Phaeacians would sit and eat and drink, for there was plenty the whole year round. And on their pedestals stood golden statues of young men, holding lit torches in their hands, to light the hall by night for those at the feast. Fifty serving women work in that house: some grind the golden grain at the millstones, others weave at the loom or sit and spin, their hands fluttering like the leaves of a tall poplar; and the linen they weave is so close that the oil runs off it. For just as the Phaeacian men are the finest sailors in the world, so their women are the finest at the loom — Athena has given them beyond all others a gift for the lovely work of her hands, and good sense as well.

Outside the courtyard gate, hard by the doors, lies a great orchard of four acres, with a hedge running all the way around it. Tall trees grow there in full leaf — pears and pomegranates and apples bright with fruit, sweet figs and olives in their prime. The fruit of these trees never spoils and never fails, winter or summer, the whole year through; the West Wind blows over them always, bringing some to bud while it ripens others. Pear ripens on pear, apple on apple, cluster on cluster of grapes, and fig on fig. There too is rooted a fruitful vineyard. Part of it lies open to the sun on level ground, drying in the heat; in another part the men are picking the grapes, and in another treading them out, while the near rows are still shedding their blossom and the far ones just beginning to darken. And along the lowest edge grow trim beds of every kind of flower, in bloom from one year's end to the next. Two springs run through it: one is led in channels across the whole garden, while the other slips beneath the courtyard gate toward the high house itself, and from it the townspeople draw their water. Such were the splendid gifts the gods had heaped on the house of Alcinous.

There godlike Odysseus stood a while and gazed. And when his heart had taken its fill of wonder, he crossed the threshold quickly and went inside. He found the Phaeacian leaders and chief men pouring libations from their cups to keen-eyed Hermes, the slayer of Argos — the last offering they made each night before turning to sleep. Straight through the hall went Odysseus, still wrapped in the thick mist Athena had laid about him, until he reached Arete and King Alcinous. He threw his arms about Arete's knees — and in that instant the magical mist fell away from him, and there he was, in plain sight. The whole company froze in silence, struck dumb at the sight of a man among them; and Odysseus began his plea at once.

"Arete," he said, "daughter of great Rhexenor — after all I have suffered, I come as a suppliant to your knees, and to your husband, and to these men at your feast. May the gods grant them good lives, and may each pass on to his children the wealth in his halls and the honor the people have given him. But I beg you, see me sent home to my own land, and quickly — for I have been long away from my friends, and long in grief."

With that he sat down on the hearth, in the ashes by the fire, and no one said a word. At last the old hero Echeneus spoke — the eldest of the Phaeacians, a fine speaker who knew the wisdom of long years — and out of an honest heart he said:

"Alcinous, this does you no credit — to let a stranger sit on the ground among the hearth-ashes while the rest of us hold back, waiting on your word. Come, raise the man up and seat him on a silver-studded chair, and tell your heralds to mix more wine, so we may pour an offering to Zeus who hurls the thunder, who walks beside every suppliant who comes in honor. And let the housekeeper give our guest a supper out of what the house has."

When Alcinous heard this, the strong and sacred prince took wise Odysseus by the hand, raised him from the hearth, and gave him the chair of Laodamas — the favorite son who had been sitting beside him — bidding the boy give way. A serving woman brought water in a beautiful golden pitcher and poured it over his hands into a silver basin, and drew up a polished table beside him. A grave housekeeper brought bread and laid it out, with many good things besides, giving freely from her stores; and Odysseus, long-suffering and brilliant, ate and drank. Then Alcinous said to one of his men: "Pontonous, mix the bowl and serve it round the hall, so we may pour to Zeus who hurls the thunder, the protector of all suppliants who come in honor."
Pontonous mixed the honeyed wine and carried it round, giving each man his portion to pour. And when they had made their offerings and drunk their fill, Alcinous spoke out among them:

"Leaders and lords of the Phaeacians, hear me. You have feasted; now go home to your beds. In the morning we'll call a larger gathering of the elders, give our guest the honor of a feast, and offer fine sacrifices to the gods. After that we'll see to his passage home — so that with no toil or trouble of his own he may come, with our escort, swiftly and gladly back to his native land, however far off it lies; and may come to no harm or grief on the way, until he sets foot in his own country. There, once home, he must bear whatever fate and the heavy Spinners wove for him at his birth, the day his mother brought him into the world. But if he is one of the immortals come down from the sky, then the gods are doing something new with us — for till now they have always shown themselves to us plainly, whenever we offer them great sacrifices, and they feast at our side, sitting where we sit. And even if a lone traveler stumbles on one of them, they put on no disguise, for we are close kin to the gods, as the Cyclopes are, and the wild tribes of the Giants."

Then Odysseus, full of schemes, answered him: "Alcinous, put that thought out of your mind. I am nothing like the immortals who hold the wide heaven, not in body or in spirit — I am only a mortal man. Think of those you know who carry the heaviest load of sorrow; those are the ones I would set myself beside in suffering. Indeed, I could tell you a longer tale of misery still, of all I have endured by the will of the gods. But for now, let me eat my supper for all my grief. There is nothing so shameless as the belly — it forces a man to take notice of it, no matter how worn down he is or how deep his sorrow runs. My heart is heavy with grief, yet the belly keeps ordering me to eat and drink, driving the memory of all I've suffered clean out of me, and demanding only to be filled. But you — at the first light of dawn, set about sending a poor man home to his own land, hard as my trials have been. And then let life leave me, if only I may first see my own house again, my servants, and my great high-roofed halls."

So he spoke, and they all approved his words and called for the stranger to be given his escort home, since all he said was fair and right. Then, when they had poured their offerings and drunk their fill, each man went home to his own house to sleep, leaving Odysseus behind in the hall with Arete and godlike Alcinous, while the serving women cleared away the supper things. Arete was the first to speak, for she had recognized the cloak and tunic and the fine clothes Odysseus was wearing — she and her women had woven them with their own hands. So she said to him, winged words: "Stranger, there is one thing I will ask you first, myself. Who are you, and where are your people? And who gave you these clothes? Didn't you say you came here drifting over the sea?"

And Odysseus, full of schemes, answered her: "It would be a long story, my queen, to tell the whole tale of my troubles end to end, for the gods of heaven have given me many. But I'll tell you what you ask. Far off in the sea there is an island called Ogygia, where Calypso lives — daughter of Atlas, a goddess cunning and dangerous, with her lovely braided hair. She lives apart, and no one comes to her, god or mortal. But some god brought me alone to her hearth, broken, after Zeus split my swift ship with his bright bolt and shattered it in the middle of the wine-dark sea. All my brave companions drowned, every one; I alone caught hold of the keel and was carried nine days adrift, until on the tenth black night the gods washed me ashore on Ogygia, where Calypso lives. She took me in, and treated me with all kindness, and tended me, and would have made me deathless and ageless all my days — but she could never win over the heart in my breast.

"There I stayed with her seven full years, and I soaked with my tears the immortal clothes she gave me, the whole time through. But when the eighth year came round at last, she herself ordered me off and urged me to go — whether some word came from Zeus, or her own heart had turned. She sent me away on a raft of bound timbers, well stocked with bread and sweet wine, and put good clothes on my back, and sent a warm, fair wind behind me. Seventeen days I sailed across the open sea, and on the eighteenth the shadowy mountains of your land rose into view — and my heart leaped, unlucky as I was. Yet there was still much suffering ahead of me. For now Poseidon the earth-shaker raised a great storm against me and barred my way; he stirred the sea so high that I could no longer hold to my raft, and it broke apart under the fury of the wind, and I had to swim for it, until at last the wind and the current drove me to your shore.

"There I tried to come to land, but the surf hurled me against the rocks — it was a cruel place — so I drew back and swam on, until I came to a river that looked the kindest landing of all: no rocks, and sheltered from the wind. I dragged myself out and lay there, gathering my strength again, while the holy night came on. I climbed up from the river, into a thicket, and heaped the leaves over me, and a god poured a deep sleep over my eyes. There among the leaves, sick at heart, I slept the whole night through and on past dawn, until the sun was sinking toward the west and woke me. And I saw your daughter's serving women playing on the sand, and the girl herself among them, like a goddess. To her I made my prayer — and she showed a wisdom you would never look for in one so young, for the young are usually thoughtless. She gave me plenty of bread and sparkling wine, and had me bathed in the river, and gave me these clothes. That is the whole of it — the truth, told plainly, for all the pain in telling it."
Then Alcinous answered him: "Stranger, my daughter did fall short in one thing — she should have brought you straight here to our house with her women, since you had turned to her first for help."

"Don't blame her for it, my lord," Odysseus answered. "The fault is not hers. She did tell me to follow along with the women — but I held back, out of shame, and out of fear that the sight of me might anger you. We mortals are quick to take offense, every one of us."

"Stranger," said Alcinous, "I'm not the kind of man to flare up over nothing. In all things the right measure is the better way. By Father Zeus, and Athena, and Apollo — seeing the man you are, and how your mind runs with my own, I could wish you would stay here, and take my daughter to wife, and be called my son-in-law. I would give you a house and lands of your own, if you chose to stay. But against your will, no Phaeacian shall keep you — Zeus forbid it. And to set your mind at rest, I name the day now: tomorrow I will see to your passage home. You may sleep the whole way over, while my men row you across smooth water to your own country, or wherever you please — even somewhere far beyond Euboea, which those of my people who saw it, the day they carried fair-haired Rhadamanthus to visit Tityus the son of Earth, call the farthest land of all. Even there they went and came back in a single day, and felt no strain. You'll see for yourself how my ships are the best there are, and what splendid oarsmen my young men make."

At that godlike Odysseus rejoiced, and lifted up a prayer: "Father Zeus, grant that Alcinous may do all he has promised. Then his name will never die among men on the grain-giving earth — and I will come home to my own land."

So they spoke together. Then white-armed Arete told her women to set a bed up under the gateway gallery, to lay fine purple rugs on it and spread coverlets over them, with thick woolen blankets to throw on top. The women went out of the hall with torches in their hands, and when they had made the bed snug, they came to Odysseus and roused him: "Come now, stranger, and sleep — your bed is ready." And glad indeed he was to lie down to his rest.
So Odysseus, long-suffering and brilliant, slept there on the corded bed under the echoing gallery; but Alcinous lay down in the inner room of the high house, and the queen his wife beside him.
books.title: The Palace of Alcinous

books.label: Book VIII
paragraphs: When the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn, appeared, mighty Alcinous rose from his bed, and so did Odysseus, sacker of cities. Alcinous led the way to the Phaeacian meeting-place, which was laid out beside the ships, and there the two of them sat down side by side on benches of polished stone. Meanwhile Pallas Athena went up and down the town in the likeness of one of wise Alcinous' heralds, busy on her plan to bring Odysseus home. She went up to each man in turn and said: "Come now, you captains and counselors of the Phaeacians — come to the assembly, all of you, and hear the stranger who has just come to the house of King Alcinous after long wandering on the sea. He looks like one of the immortal gods."

With these words she set them all astir, and quickly the seats and the standing-room filled with the gathering crowd. Many a man marveled at the sight of clever Odysseus, for Athena had shed a wondrous grace over his head and shoulders, and made him look taller and broader than before, so that he might win the goodwill of the Phaeacians and come through all the trials of strength to which they would challenge him. When they had all come together, Alcinous stood and spoke:

"Hear me, captains and counselors of the Phaeacians, and let me say what is on my mind. This stranger — I do not know who he is — has come wandering to my house from somewhere out of the East or the West. He asks for passage home, and begs us to make it certain. So let us speed him on his way, as we have sped others before him; for no one who ever came to this house has had to linger long, grieving for want of an escort. Come — let us drag a black ship down to the bright sea, one that has never yet made a voyage, and pick fifty-two of our finest young men to crew her. When you have lashed the oars to the thole-pins, leave the ship and come up to my house and make ready a feast in haste; I will provide for all of you. These are my orders to the young men who will sail. As for you lords who carry the staff, come to my fine halls, so that we may welcome the stranger there — I will take no refusal. And call in godlike Demodocus, the bard; the god has given him the gift of song above all others, to gladden us with whatever his heart moves him to sing."

So he spoke, and led the way, and the staff-bearing lords followed, while a herald went to fetch the divine singer. The fifty-two chosen oarsmen went down to the shore of the restless sea, as they had been told, and when they reached the ship and the water they dragged the black hull into the deep, set the mast and the sails inside her, lashed the oars in their leather loops in good order, and spread the white sails aloft. They moored her well out from the land, and then came up to the great house of wise Alcinous. The galleries and the courts and the walled grounds were thronged with the crowds that gathered, young and old alike. For them Alcinous slaughtered a dozen sheep, eight white-tusked boars, and two shambling oxen; these they skinned and dressed and made ready, and laid out a glad feast.

Then the herald came near, leading the faithful bard, Demodocus, whom the Muse had loved above all men, though she had given him both good and evil: she had taken the light from his eyes, but granted him the gift of sweet song. Pontonous set a silver-studded chair for him in the middle of the guests, leaning it against a tall pillar; and the herald hung the clear-toned lyre on a peg above his head, and showed him with his hands how to reach for it. Beside him he set a fine table and a basket of bread, and a cup of wine, to drink whenever his heart desired.

So they reached out their hands to the good things spread before them, and when they had taken their fill of food and drink, the Muse stirred the bard to sing of the famous deeds of men — a tale whose fame had then climbed all the way to the wide heaven: the quarrel between Odysseus and Achilles, son of Peleus, and the savage words they had hurled at each other one day as they sat at the gods' feast. Agamemnon, king of men, had been glad in his heart to see the best of the Greeks at each other's throats; for Phoebus Apollo had foretold it to him at holy Delphi, when he crossed the stone threshold to consult the oracle. There, by the will of Zeus, had begun the rolling wave of ruin that broke over Greeks and Trojans alike.

So the famous bard sang, but Odysseus took his great purple cloak in his strong hands and drew it up over his head and hid his handsome face, for he was ashamed to let the Phaeacians see the tears welling under his brows. Each time the divine singer paused, Odysseus would wipe the tears away, lower the cloak from his head, and lift his two-handled cup and pour an offering to the gods. But every time the bard began again — for the Phaeacian lords kept urging him on, they loved his song so — Odysseus would cover his head and weep. No one in all that company noticed his tears but Alcinous, who sat close beside him and caught the deep, heavy sighs he was heaving. At once the king spoke up to the Phaeacians, who love their oars: "Hear me, captains and counselors of the Phaeacians. By now our hearts have had their fill of the shared feast and of the lyre, the feast's true companion. Let us go out now and try our hand at every kind of contest, so that when our guest reaches home he can tell his friends how far we outstrip all other men as boxers and wrestlers, as jumpers and as runners."

With that he led the way, and the others followed. A herald hung the clear-toned lyre back on its peg, took Demodocus by the hand, and led him out of the hall, along the same road that the noblest Phaeacians were taking to look on at the games. They went out to the gathering-ground, and a great crowd, past counting, came after them, and many fine young men stood up to compete. Acroneos rose, and Ocyalus and Elatreus, Nauteus and Prymneus, Anchialus and Eretmeus, Ponteus and Proreus, Thoon and Anabesineus, and Amphialus, son of Polyneus, son of Tecton. Up too stood Euryalus, son of Naubolus, the equal of murderous Ares himself, and the best-looking man among all the Phaeacians but for flawless Laodamas. And three sons of great Alcinous rose as well: Laodamas, Halius, and godlike Clytoneus.

First they ran the foot-race. The line was drawn for them from the post, and they all flew forward together, raising the dust across the plain. Godlike Clytoneus came in first, far ahead — by as much ground as a team of mules can break in a fallow field, that far he left the rest behind and reached the crowd. Next they tried the hard work of wrestling, and there Euryalus came out best of all. Amphialus was the finest at the jump; at the discus, no one came near Elatreus; and at boxing, Laodamas, the noble son of Alcinous, was the best. And when they had all gladdened their hearts with the games, Laodamas, son of Alcinous, said: "Friends, come, let us ask the stranger whether he is skilled in any sport. He is no mean figure to look at — his thighs and his calves, his two hands, his thick neck, all of him is built for strength. And he is not past his prime; it is only that he is broken by his many hardships. There is nothing, I tell you, like the sea for grinding a man down, however strong he may be."
And Euryalus answered him: "Laodamas, you have spoken well, and to the point. Go up to him yourself, then, and put it to him."

When the good son of Alcinous heard this, he went and stood in the middle of the crowd and said to Odysseus: "Come, sir, you too — will you try your hand at our games, if you have any skill in them? And surely you must; there is no glory for a man in all his days greater than what he wins with his own hands and feet. Come, then, and make a trial of it, and shake the sorrow from your heart. Your journey home will not be long delayed now; the ship is already drawn down to the water, and the crew is ready."

Then resourceful Odysseus answered him: "Laodamas, why do you taunt me with this? My heart is set on grief, not games. I have suffered more than I can say, and I sit here among you now as a suppliant, begging your king and your people to send me home."

But Euryalus spoke up and threw the insult in his face: "No — I can see it now: you are no man for the kind of contests men love. You are some skipper of a tramping merchant crew, a man who minds his cargo and keeps his eye on his freight and his greedy profits. There is nothing of the athlete about you."

Then resourceful Odysseus looked at him from under his brows and said: "Stranger, that was an ugly thing to say. You talk like a reckless fool. So it is — the gods do not give every grace to every man, not beauty, not brains, not eloquence all at once. One man is poor enough to look at, but the god crowns his words with such grace that men gaze at him with delight; he speaks on without a stumble, with a winning modesty, and stands out in any gathering, and when he walks through the town men look on him as on a god. Another has the beauty of the immortals, but no grace is set as a crown upon his words. That is your case. You are splendid to look at — a god could not improve you — but your wits are worthless. You have stirred the heart in my breast with your rude, ill-judged talk. I am no stranger to games, whatever you think — no, I was among the best of them while I still had my youth and the strength in my hands. But now I am held down by hardship and grief; I have come through much, cutting my way through wars among men and across the cruel waves. Still, for all I have suffered, I will try your contests. Your words have bitten deep, and you have goaded me to it."

He sprang up, cloak and all, without even stripping, and seized a discus — a bigger one, more massive, far heavier than the ones the Phaeacians threw among themselves. He whirled it back and let it fly from his great hand, and the stone hummed in the air; and the long-oared Phaeacians, those famous seamen, cringed down to the ground beneath the rush of it as it flew. Easily, smoothly, it sailed past the marks of every other throw. Athena, taking the form of a man, marked the spot where it had fallen, and called out to him: "Stranger, even a blind man could find your mark by feeling for it, for it is not lost in the crowd of the others — it lies far out, ahead of them all. Take heart in this contest, at least. No Phaeacian will reach this throw, or beat it."

So she spoke, and long-suffering, brilliant Odysseus was glad, glad to find a true friend among the onlookers, and now he spoke to the Phaeacians with a lighter heart: "Match that, young men, if you can — and I think I will throw another, as far or farther. As for the rest, if any man's heart and spirit move him, let him come and try me — you have stung me past bearing — at boxing, at wrestling, at the foot-race, I care not which. Any man of you all but Laodamas; for he is my host, and who would fight against the man who has befriended him? Only a fool, a man worth nothing, would challenge his host to a contest in a foreign land; he would be cutting the ground from under his own feet. But of the rest I refuse no one and make light of none; I will meet any man face to face and learn what he is made of. There is no sport men know that I am bad at. I know my way well with the polished bow: in a press of enemies, I would be the first to find my man with an arrow, though a whole crowd of comrades stood beside me shooting too. Of all the men now alive on the earth and eating bread, Philoctetes alone outshot me, when we Greeks drew the bow before Troy. But I will not set myself against the men of long ago — against Heracles, or against Eurytus of Oechalia, who would draw the bow even against the immortals. That is how great Eurytus came to his early death; he never reached old age in his halls, for Apollo killed him in anger, because the man had dared to challenge him at the bow. And with a spear I can throw farther than any other man can shoot an arrow. Only at the foot-race do I fear that one of you Phaeacians might pass me; the sea has worn me down past all decency, for there was no steady food aboard for me — and so my limbs are slack."

So he spoke, and they all fell silent. Only Alcinous found his voice and answered him: "Stranger, there is no offense in anything you say. You wish to show the prowess that is in you, since this man stood up beside you in the games and insulted you — and no one who knew how to speak with sense would ever belittle your prowess. But now hear me, so that you may tell your story to some other hero when you are home, dining in your own hall beside your wife and children, and so remember the skill that is ours, the deeds that Zeus has set in our hands ever since our fathers' time. We are no great boxers, no, nor wrestlers, but we are quick of foot, and the finest of seamen, and dear to us forever are the feast, the lyre, the dance, fresh clothes to wear, the warm bath, and our beds. Come, then — let those of you who are the best dancers of the Phaeacians make your play, so that when our guest reaches home he can tell his friends how far we surpass all other men, at sailing and at running, at the dance and at song. And someone go quickly and fetch Demodocus his clear-toned lyre; it is lying somewhere in my halls."

So godlike Alcinous spoke, and a herald rose to bring the hollow lyre from the king's house. And the nine chosen judges stood up, the public officers who saw to everything at the games; they smoothed the dancing-floor and opened a fair, wide ring. The herald came back with the clear-toned lyre for Demodocus, who stepped into the middle, and around him stood young men in the first bloom of their strength, masters of the dance. They struck their feet on the holy floor, and Odysseus watched the flashing of their feet and marveled in his heart.

Then, striking the strings, the bard lifted his voice in a beautiful song — of the love of Ares and Aphrodite of the lovely crown, and how they first lay together in secret in the house of Hephaestus. Many were the gifts Ares gave her, and he shamed the bed and the marriage of lord Hephaestus. But Helios the Sun saw them at their love and went and told him. And when Hephaestus heard the bitter news, he went to his forge with murder in his heart, and set his great anvil on its block, and hammered out chains that could not be broken or loosed, to hold the two of them fast where they lay. And when he had forged his snare, raging at Ares, he went into the room where his own bed stood and bound the netting of chains all around the bedposts, and let many of them hang down from the great roof-beam above — fine as a spider's web, so fine that no one could see them, not even one of the blessed gods, so cunningly had they been made. When he had spread the whole trap over the bed, he made as if to set out for Lemnos, that strong-walled town that of all places on earth he loved the best. And Ares of the golden reins kept no idle watch; the moment he saw the great craftsman Hephaestus go, he made for the famous god's house, hot with longing for Aphrodite of the lovely crown.

She had only just come home from her father, the mighty son of Kronos, and had sat down. Ares came into the house and took her by the hand and spoke to her, calling her by name: "Come, my love, let us go to bed and take our pleasure lying down. Hephaestus is not at home; by now, I think, he has gone off to Lemnos, among the Sintians, whose speech is harsh and strange."

So he spoke, and to her it seemed a welcome thing to lie with him. So the two of them went to the bed and lay down — and around them the chains that cunning Hephaestus had forged came crashing down, so that they could not move a limb or raise themselves at all, and they knew, too late, that there was no escaping. And the famous god with the crooked feet came near; he had turned back before reaching the land of Lemnos, for Helios the Sun had kept his watch and brought him word. Sick at heart, he came to his own house, and stood there in the doorway, and a wild fury seized him. He gave a terrible shout, and cried out to all the gods:

"Father Zeus, and all you other blessed gods who live forever — come here and see a thing to laugh at, a thing past all bearing: how Aphrodite, the daughter of Zeus, dishonors me always, lame as I am, and gives her love to deadly Ares, because he is handsome and sound of foot, while I was born a cripple. And no one is to blame for that but my own two parents — would they had never had me! Come and look where the two of them lie, in love, climbed into my own bed; it cuts me to the heart to see it. And yet I do not think they will want to lie like that much longer, in love as they are. Soon enough they will lose all desire to sleep — but the trap and the chains will hold them fast, until her father pays me back every last gift I handed over for this shameless girl. His daughter is beautiful, yes — but she cannot keep faith."

So he spoke, and the gods came thronging to the bronze-floored house. Poseidon came, who holds the earth in his arms; and Hermes came, the bringer of luck; and lord Apollo came, who works from far off. But the goddesses, every one of them, stayed home for shame. So the gods, the givers of good things, stood there in the doorway, and unquenchable laughter broke out among the blessed gods as they looked on the craft of clever Hephaestus. And one of them would glance at the god beside him and say:

"Bad deeds don't prosper. The slow catches the swift — see how Hephaestus, slow as he is, and lame, has caught Ares with his craft, the fastest of all the gods on Olympus. Now Ares owes the fine an adulterer pays."

So they spoke to one another. But lord Apollo, son of Zeus, said to Hermes: "Hermes, son of Zeus, runner and giver of good things — would you be willing to lie under all those crushing chains, if you could sleep at the side of golden Aphrodite?"

And the keen-eyed slayer of Argos answered him: "If only it could be so, lord Apollo, archer from afar! Let there be three times as many chains, past counting, and let all of you gods look on, and all the goddesses too — I would still sleep at golden Aphrodite's side."

So he spoke, and laughter rose among the deathless gods. But Poseidon did not laugh; he kept pleading with Hephaestus, the great craftsman, to set Ares free. He spoke to him with winged words: "Let him go, and I give you my word that he will pay you in full, all that is right and fitting, before the deathless gods."

But the famous god with the crooked feet answered him: "Poseidon, who holds the earth — do not ask this of me. The pledges of a worthless man are worthless to hold. How could I bind you before the deathless gods, if Ares should slip away and leave both his debt and his chains behind him?"

Then Poseidon the earth-shaker answered him: "Hephaestus — if Ares does run off and leave his debt unpaid, I myself will pay you." And the famous god with the crooked feet replied: "Then it is not right, and it is not possible, to refuse you." With that the mighty Hephaestus loosed the chains, and the two of them, the moment they were free of that strong bond, sprang up at once and were gone — Ares away to Thrace, and laughter-loving Aphrodite to Cyprus, to Paphos, where she has her sacred ground and her altar fragrant with incense. There the Graces bathed her and rubbed her with the immortal oil that glistens on the everlasting gods, and dressed her in lovely clothes, a wonder to behold.
So sang the famous bard, and Odysseus was glad at heart to hear it, and so were the long-oared Phaeacians, those famous seamen.

Then Alcinous called on Halius and Laodamas to dance by themselves, for there was no one who could match them. They took a fine ball, a purple one that skilled Polybus had made for them, and one of them would arch backward and fling it high toward the shadowy clouds, while the other would leap clear of the ground and catch it easily before his feet came down again. And when they had shown what they could do throwing the ball straight up, they began to dance on the bounteous earth, tossing it back and forth between them, while the rest of the young men stood about the ring and beat the time, and a great drumming of feet rose up. Then brilliant Odysseus said to Alcinous: "Lord Alcinous, most renowned of men — you told me your dancers were the best in the world, and now I see it is the plain truth. The wonder of it holds me as I watch."

So he spoke, and the mighty king Alcinous was delighted, and at once said to the Phaeacians, who love their oars: "Hear me, captains and counselors of the Phaeacians. This stranger seems to me a man of fine good sense. Come, then — let us give him a guest-gift, as is only right. Twelve lords hold sway and rule among our people, and I am the thirteenth. Let each of us bring him a fresh cloak and a tunic and a talent of fine gold, and let us gather all of it together quickly, so that the stranger may take it in his own hands and go to his supper with a glad heart. And as for Euryalus — let him make it right with the man himself, with words and with a gift, for what he said was out of all bounds."

So he spoke, and they all agreed and gave the order, and each sent his herald off to fetch the gift. Then Euryalus answered the king and said: "Lord Alcinous, most renowned of men — I will make it right with the stranger, as you ask. I will give him this sword, all of bronze, with a hilt of silver, and a scabbard of fresh-sawn ivory closing round it. It will be worth much to him."

With that he put the silver-studded sword into the hands of Odysseus and spoke to him with winged words: "Good fortune to you, honored stranger. If any harsh word slipped from me, let the storm-winds catch it up and carry it off, and may the gods grant that you see your wife again and reach your own land, for you have been long away from your dear ones, and have borne much sorrow."

And resourceful Odysseus answered him: "And good fortune to you too, my friend, and may the gods grant you every blessing. And may you never, in days to come, miss this sword you have given me with your words of peace." So he spoke, and slung the silver-studded sword about his shoulders.

The sun went down, and the splendid gifts began to arrive, as the proud heralds carried them to the house of Alcinous. There the sons of flawless Alcinous took them and laid the lovely treasures before their honored mother. The king led the way, and the others followed, and they came in and sat down on the high seats. Then mighty Alcinous said to Arete: "Wife, bring out the finest chest we have, and lay in it a fresh cloak and a tunic. And heat a cauldron of water over the fire for the stranger, so that when he has bathed and seen all the gifts that the noble Phaeacians have brought packed away in good order, he may take his pleasure in the feast and in the singing that follows. And I will give him this cup of mine, beautiful and golden, so that he may remember me all his days, whenever he pours an offering in his hall to Zeus and the other gods."

So he spoke, and Arete told her serving-women to set a great three-legged cauldron over the fire as fast as they could. They set the cauldron for the bath on the blazing fire, poured the water in, and piled on wood to make it burn, and the flame licked round the cauldron's belly and the water grew hot. Meanwhile Arete brought a beautiful chest from her own room for the stranger, and packed into it the fine gifts of clothing and gold that the Phaeacians had given, and added a cloak and a good tunic of her own, and spoke to him with winged words: "See to the lid yourself now, and tie it fast with a good knot, so that no one robs you on the way, when you are sleeping your sweet sleep aboard the black ship."

When long-suffering, brilliant Odysseus heard this, at once he fitted the lid in place and tied it fast with a cunning knot that the lady Circe had once taught him. And straightway the housekeeper called him to step into the bath and wash. Glad was his heart at the sight of the warm bath, for such comforts had not often come his way since he left the home of lovely-haired Calypso — though there, while it lasted, he had been cared for like a god. When the serving-women had bathed him and rubbed him with oil, and dressed him in a fine cloak and tunic, he came out of the bath and went to join the men over their wine. And Nausicaa, with her god-given beauty, stood beside the pillar that held up the roof of the hall, and marveled at Odysseus as her eyes fell on him. She spoke to him with winged words: "Farewell, stranger. And when you are home in your own land, remember me sometimes, for it is to me, first of all, that you owe the price of your life."

And resourceful Odysseus answered her: "Nausicaa, daughter of great-hearted Alcinous — may Zeus grant it, the loud-thundering lord, husband of Hera, that I reach my home and see the day of my return. Then, even there, I will pray to you as to a god, all my days; for it was you, girl, who gave me back my life."

He spoke, and sat down on the chair beside King Alcinous. By now they were serving out the portions and mixing the wine, and a herald came near, leading the faithful bard, Demodocus, honored by all the people. He seated him in the middle of the company, leaning the chair against a tall pillar. Then resourceful Odysseus called to a herald, cutting off a portion of the chine of a white-tusked boar — and plenty of it, with the rich fat still on either side: "Herald, here, take this meat to Demodocus, so that he may eat; I would show him my goodwill, sorrow as I am. Among all the men who walk the earth, bards are owed their share of honor and respect, for the Muse has taught them the paths of song, and she loves the whole tribe of singers."

So he spoke, and the herald carried it over and put it into the hands of the hero Demodocus, who took it and was glad at heart. Then they reached out their hands to the good things spread before them, and when they had taken their fill of food and drink, resourceful Odysseus said to Demodocus: "Demodocus, I praise you above all mortal men. Either the Muse, daughter of Zeus, has taught you, or Apollo himself — for you sing the fate of the Greeks so truly, all that they did and suffered and toiled through, as though you had been there yourself, or heard it from one who was. Come now, change your song, and sing of the building of the wooden horse, which Epeus made with Athena's help — the cunning thing that brilliant Odysseus brought up into the citadel as a trap, after he had filled it with the men who sacked Troy. Sing me that, sing it as it truly happened, and I will declare to all the world that the god has freely given you the gift of holy song."

So he spoke, and the bard, stirred by the god, took up the tale and let his song flow — beginning where the Greeks had boarded their well-benched ships and sailed away, after setting fire to their own huts, while the others, with famous Odysseus, sat already hidden inside the horse in the Trojans' own meeting-place; for the Trojans themselves had dragged it up into their citadel. So it stood there, and the people sat around it arguing endlessly, of three minds about what to do: whether to split the hollow timber open with the pitiless bronze, or to haul it to the high rock and hurl it down the cliff, or to let it stand as a great offering to win the gods' favor — and that was the way it ended, for it was fated that the city should fall once it had taken in that great horse of wood, where all the best of the Greeks sat waiting to bring death and doom upon the Trojans. And he sang how the sons of the Greeks poured out of the horse, leaving their hollow ambush, and sacked the steep city. He sang how this man and that laid waste the town from one quarter to another, and how Odysseus went like the war-god Ares, with godlike Menelaus, to the house of Deiphobus. There, he sang, Odysseus dared his most terrible fight, and won it in the end through the help of great-hearted Athena.

All this the famous bard sang. But Odysseus felt the grief melt his heart, and the tears ran down and wet his cheeks. He wept the way a woman weeps, throwing her arms about her own dear husband, who has fallen in front of his city and his people, fighting to keep the pitiless day from his town and his children. She has seen him gasping in his death, and she pours herself over him, wailing aloud, while behind her the enemy strike her back and her shoulders with their spear-shafts and lead her away into slavery, to a life of toil and misery, and her cheeks waste with the most pitiful grief — even so pitifully did the tears run down from under Odysseus' brows. And again no one in all the company noticed his weeping but Alcinous, who sat close beside him and caught the deep, heavy sighs he was heaving. At once the king spoke up to the Phaeacians, who love their oars:

"Hear me, captains and counselors of the Phaeacians. Let Demodocus hold back the clear-toned lyre now, for his song does not please everyone here alike. From the moment we sat down to supper and the divine singer began, our guest has never once left off his bitter grieving; some great sorrow has surely closed over his heart. So let the bard leave off, and let us all be glad together, hosts and guest alike; that is the better way. For all of this — the escort and the gifts of friendship we so gladly give — is in honor of our guest, and any man with even a grain of sense knows that a suppliant and a stranger are to be treated like a brother.

"And so, my friend, do not hide from me, with cunning thoughts, the thing I am about to ask you; it is far better to speak it out. Tell me the name your father and mother called you back home, and the people of your town and the country round about; for no one among men, whether highborn or low, is altogether without a name once he is born — every parent gives a child a name at birth. And tell me your land, your people, and your city, so that our ships may carry you there with their own minds set on the course. For the Phaeacian ships have no pilots, and no steering-oars such as other ships have; they know of themselves the thoughts and the wishes of men, and they know all the cities and rich fields of every people, and they cross the gulf of the sea at the greatest speed, wrapped in mist and cloud, and never any fear of harm or wreck. And yet I once heard my father Nausithous say that Poseidon held a grudge against us, because we give safe passage to every man without harm — that one day he would shatter a fine Phaeacian ship as it came home from such an escort, out on the misty sea, and would throw up a great mountain to hide our city. So the old man said; the god may bring it to pass, or leave it undone, as it pleases his heart.

"But come now, tell me this, and tell me truly: where have your wanderings carried you? What countries of men have you seen — their great cities, the people themselves? Who among them were cruel and savage and lawless, and who were kind to strangers and god-fearing of mind? And tell me too why you weep and grieve in your heart when you hear the fate of the Greeks who went to Troy. The gods themselves brought all that to pass; they spun out the death of those men so that there might be a song for those yet to be born. Did some kinsman of yours, by marriage, fall before Troy — a brave man — a son-in-law, or a father-in-law, the dearest of those who are bound to us outside our own blood? Or was it some comrade, dear to your heart, a man of valor? For a true friend, sound in his thinking, is no less dear to a man than his own brother."
books.title: The Games of the Phaeacians

books.label: Book IX
paragraphs: Then resourceful Odysseus answered him: "King Alcinous, most renowned of men, it is a fine thing indeed to listen to a bard with such a god-given voice as this man has. To my mind there is nothing better or sweeter than when a whole people keeps holiday together, the feasters sitting in good order through the hall to hear the singer, the tables piled with bread and meat, and the steward drawing wine from the bowl and carrying it round to fill every cup. That, I think, is as fair a sight as a man can see. But you have set your heart on asking me about my own bitter troubles, and so wake fresh grief in me as I tell them. Where, then, shall I begin, and where leave off? For the gods have given me sorrows beyond counting.

"First of all, I will tell you my name, so that you too may know it, and so that, if I live out this time of suffering, I may be your guest-friend in days to come, far off as my home lies. I am Odysseus, son of Laertes, known among all men for my cunning, and my fame reaches the heavens. I live in Ithaca, where there is a high mountain, Neriton, shaking its forests in the wind; and round it lie other islands, close to one another — Dulichium, Same, and wooded Zacynthus. Ithaca itself lies low, the farthest out to sea of them all, off toward the dark, while the rest face the dawn and the rising sun. It is a rugged island, but it raises good men, and for myself I know of no sweeter sight than my own country. The goddess Calypso kept me with her in her hollow cave, longing to make me her husband; and so too did the cunning Aeaean witch, Circe, who wanted me for hers. But neither of them could win my heart. There is nothing dearer to a man than his own land and his own parents; let him live in the richest house in the world, far away, cut off from his father and mother, and it gives him no joy. But come — let me tell you of the hard and bitter journey home that Zeus laid on me when I sailed from Troy.

"The wind carried me first from Troy to Ismarus, the city of the Cicones. There I sacked the town and killed the men. We carried off their wives and a great store of plunder, and shared it out so fairly that no man went without his portion. Then I urged my men to be off, and quickly — but the fools would not listen. They stayed there on the beach, drinking deep of the wine and slaughtering whole flocks of sheep and herds of cattle by the sea. Meanwhile the Cicones who had escaped cried out to other Cicones, their neighbors inland, who were more in number and braver, men skilled in fighting from chariots and, when they had to, on foot as well. In the morning they came down on us thick as the leaves and flowers of spring, and the hand of Zeus was heavy on us; doom had marked us out for a hard day. They drew up their line of battle by the swift ships, and we hurled our bronze-tipped spears at one another. All morning, while the holy daylight gathered, we held our ground against them, outnumbered though we were; but when the sun wheeled down toward the hour the ox is loosed from the plow, the Cicones broke us and turned us back, and we lost six strong-greaved men from every ship. The rest of us got away, glad to be alive.

"From there we sailed on with grief in our hearts, glad to have come through with our own lives but mourning the dear comrades we had lost. And I would not let the curved ships go on until we had called out three times, each by name, to every one of our friends who had died there on the field, cut down by the Cicones. Then Zeus drove the North Wind against us, a screaming gale, and hid land and sea alike under his clouds, and night came rushing down out of heaven. The ships ran headlong before it, and the force of the wind tore our sails to shreds, three and four ways across. In terror of going under we hauled them down and rowed hard for the shore, and there we lay two days and two nights, our strength worn out, our hearts eaten with grief. But when fair-haired Dawn brought the third day, we stepped the masts again, spread the white sails, and sat back while the wind and the steersmen held our course. And I would have come home safe and sound, but as I was rounding Cape Malea the swell and the current and the North Wind beat me back and drove me wide of Cythera.
