"For nine days the deadly winds carried me across the teeming sea, and on the tenth we made the land of the Lotus-Eaters, a people who live on a flowering food. We went ashore there and drew fresh water, and the crews took their meal beside the swift ships. When we had eaten and drunk, I sent two of my men ahead, with a third for a runner, to find out what kind of people lived in that country. They went off and mixed with the Lotus-Eaters, who meant them no harm but gave them the lotus to taste — and any man who ate that honey-sweet fruit lost all wish to bring back word or to come home again. They wanted only to stay there among the Lotus-Eaters, grazing on the lotus, and let all thought of home slip away. I dragged them back to the ships by force, weeping as they went, and bound them fast beneath the benches. Then I ordered the rest of my trusty men to hurry aboard, before any of them should taste the lotus and forget the way home. They came at once and took their places, and beat the grey sea white with their oars.

"From there we sailed on, sick at heart, and came to the country of the Cyclopes — a lawless, brutal people, who leave everything to the gods. They never plant with their own hands and never plow; yet the earth, untilled and unsown, brings up everything for them — wheat, barley, and vines heavy with great clusters of grapes that the rain of Zeus swells into wine. They have no councils to make laws and no meeting-places; they live on the peaks of high mountains, in hollow caves, and each one lays down the law for his own wife and children and cares nothing for his neighbors.

"Now off the harbor of that country, neither close in nor far out, there lies a wooded island, overrun with countless wild goats. No man's foot ever scares them, for no hunters trudge through its forests or toil over its ridges. It is never grazed by flocks or broken by the plow; year after year it lies empty of men, unsown and untilled, with nothing on it but the bleating goats. For the Cyclopes have no red-cheeked ships, and no shipwrights among them to build the kind of vessel that could carry them from town to town, the way other men cross the sea to one another. With ships they could have made that island fine and rich; it is no poor land, and would bear fruit in its season. Along the shore of the grey sea run soft, well-watered meadows, where the vines would never fail; there is level ground for plowing, and a man would reap a heavy harvest in due time, for the soil beneath is deep and dark. And the harbor is so snug that there is no need of moorings — no anchor-stones to throw, no cables to make fast; a man can simply run his ship ashore and wait as long as he likes, until his crew is willing and the wind turns fair. At the head of the harbor a spring of bright water runs out from under a cave, with poplars growing all around.

"It was there we put in, and some god must have guided us through the dark, for there was nothing to be seen: a thick fog lay close around the ships, and no moon shone in the sky, but lay smothered in cloud. Not one of us could make out the island with his eyes, or the long rollers breaking on the beach, until our ships ran up onto the sand itself. Then we struck the sails, stepped ashore, and lay down to sleep on the edge of the sea, waiting for the holy light of day.

"When the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn, appeared, we walked the island in wonder. And the nymphs, the daughters of Zeus who holds the storm-cloud, started up the wild mountain goats, so that my men might have their meal. At once we ran to the ships for our curved bows and our long spears, split into three bands, and let fly; and the god gave us game in plenty. I had twelve ships in my company, and to each one nine goats fell by lot, and ten to mine alone. So all that long day, until the sun went down, we sat and feasted on the rich meat and the sweet wine; for the red wine in the ships had not yet run dry — each crew had carried off a great store of it in jars when we sacked the holy city of the Cicones. And as we feasted we looked across to the land of the Cyclopes, so near at hand, and saw the smoke of their fires and heard the voices of the men and the bleating of their sheep and goats. Then, when the sun went down and darkness came on, we lay down to sleep along the breaking surf; and when rosy-fingered Dawn appeared again, I called my men together and spoke to them all:

"'The rest of you, my loyal friends, wait here. I am going across with my own ship and crew to learn what kind of men live over there — whether they are savage and lawless and cruel, or whether they fear the gods and treat a stranger kindly.'

"With that I went aboard and told my men to follow and cast off the cables. They took their places and beat the grey sea with their oars. When we reached the land — it was no long crossing — we saw a great cave near the water's edge, high on a headland and shaded over with laurels. There many flocks of sheep and goats spent the night, and around it ran a high outer wall, built of quarried stones sunk deep, and of tall pines and oaks with their crowns still on them. It was the den of a monstrous man, who pastured his flocks far off and alone, keeping clear of all others, with no law in his heart, a savage thing. He was a marvel of dread to look at — not like a man who lives on bread, but like a wooded crag that stands out on its own against the sky, high among the mountains.

"I told the rest of my trusty men to stay there and guard the ship, and chose the twelve best of them to come with me. I took along a goatskin of dark, sweet wine, which Maron, son of Euanthes, had given me — the priest of Apollo, the god who watches over Ismarus, for Maron lived within the shaded grove of the temple. When we sacked the town we had spared him, out of reverence, along with his wife and child, since he lived in the holy precinct of Phoebus Apollo; and in return he gave me splendid gifts: seven talents of well-wrought gold, a mixing-bowl all of silver, and, besides, twelve jars of wine, sweet and unmixed, a drink fit for the gods. Not one of the servants in his house knew of it, none of the maids, but only he himself, his own wife, and a single housekeeper. Whenever they drank that honey-sweet red wine, he would pour one cup of it into twenty of water, and even so a fragrance rose from the bowl so sweet and strange that it was hard to hold back from drinking. I filled a great skin with this wine and packed a leather wallet with food; for something deep in me warned, even then, that I was about to meet a man of monstrous strength, a wild thing that knew neither right nor law.

"We soon came to the cave, but found him gone — he was out pasturing his fat flocks. So we went inside and looked over everything. The drying-racks were heavy with cheeses; the pens were crowded with lambs and kids, each age penned apart — the firstlings in one fold, the middle ones in another, the newborn in a third — and all the vessels swam with whey, the pails and the bowls he milked into. At once my men began to beg me: let us take some of the cheeses and be gone, then come back quickly and drive the kids and lambs down to the swift ship and sail away. It would have been far better if we had. But I would not listen — though it would have served us well — for I wanted to see the man himself, and find out whether he would give me a guest-gift. As it turned out, his coming was no joy to my companions.

"We lit a fire, made an offering of some of the cheeses, ate of the rest, and sat down inside to wait until he should come back with his flocks. And come he did, carrying a huge load of dry wood to make his supper fire, and he flung it down inside the cave with a crash that sent us scrambling in terror to the far corner. Then he drove his fat flocks in under the roof, all the ewes he meant to milk, leaving the rams and the he-goats outside in the deep yard. After that he heaved up a great doorstone and set it in the mouth of the cave — such a stone that two and twenty good four-wheeled wagons could not have pried it from the ground, so vast was the crag he jammed against the doorway. Then he sat down and milked his ewes and bleating goats, each in turn, and set her young one under each. Half the white milk he curdled and pressed and laid by in woven baskets, and half he kept standing in the pails to drink with his supper. When he had finished all his work in haste, he kindled the fire — and only then did his eye fall on us, and he said:

"'Strangers, who are you? Where have you sailed from, over the watery ways? Are you on some trading run, or do you wander the sea at random, like raiders who risk their lives to bring trouble to other men?'

"Our hearts cracked within us at the deep boom of his voice and the sheer size of the monster. Still, I found words to answer him: 'We are Greeks, blown off our course on the way home from Troy, driven over the great gulf of the sea by every kind of wind, far from the path we meant to keep. So it has fallen out, by the will of Zeus. We are proud to be the men of Agamemnon, son of Atreus, whose fame is the greatest under heaven now, so mighty a city did he sack, so many people did he bring down. And we have come to you as suppliants, begging that you treat us with kindness, or even give us the gift a guest may rightly expect. Respect the gods, great sir; we are at your mercy. Zeus is the avenger of suppliants and strangers — Zeus the god of guests, who walks at the side of every honest traveler.'

"That was my plea, but his answer was without mercy: 'Stranger, you are a fool, or you have come from a long way off, to tell me to fear the gods and shrink from their anger. We Cyclopes care nothing for Zeus who holds the storm-cloud, or for any of the blessed gods; we are far stronger than they. I would never spare you or your men to keep out of Zeus's way — not unless my own heart moved me to it. But tell me now: where did you leave your good ship when you came ashore? Far down the coast, or close by? I should like to know.'

"He was fishing to trap me, but I knew the world too well to be caught, and I answered him with a lie of my own: 'My ship? Poseidon the earth-shaker smashed it on the rocks at the far edge of your country; he drove it against the headland, and the wind carried it in from the open sea. Only I and these few here got away from sudden death.'

"To that the cruel creature gave no answer at all. He simply lunged, shot out his hands, snatched up two of my men together, and dashed them to the ground like a pair of puppies. Their brains spilled out and wetted the earth. He hacked them limb from limb and made his supper of them, and like a mountain lion he devoured them — flesh, innards, bones, marrow — and left nothing. We could only weep and lift our hands to Zeus at the horror before our eyes, helpless to do anything else. When the Cyclops had filled his great belly with human meat and washed it down with raw milk, he stretched himself full length among his flocks inside the cave and slept. My first thought was to draw the sharp sword at my side, steal up, and drive it into his chest where the liver is cradled against the midriff, feeling for the spot with my hand. But a second thought held me back: we too would have died there, every one of us, for our own hands could never have shifted that monstrous stone he had wedged against the high doorway. So we lay there groaning, and waited for the holy dawn.

"When the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn, appeared, he kindled his fire again and milked his fine flocks, each in turn, and set her young one under each. As soon as he had finished his work in haste, he snatched up two more of my men and made his morning meal of them. Then, easily, he rolled the great stone away from the door, drove his fat flocks out, and set the stone back in its place, as lightly as a man fits the lid on a quiver. With a great whistling and shouting he turned his flocks toward the mountain, and left me there behind him, brooding on revenge — praying that Athena would grant it, and that I might pay him back.

"And of all the plans my heart turned over, this seemed the best. There lay beside one of the pens a great club of the Cyclops, green olive-wood, which he had cut to carry once it dried. To us it looked as big as the mast of a broad black ship of twenty oars, the kind that crosses the wide gulf of the sea — that long it was, and that thick. I went up to it and cut off a length the height of a man, handed it to my crew, and told them to plane it smooth; and they did. Then I sharpened the end to a point myself and hardened it in the blazing fire, and hid it away under the heaps of dung that lay thick across the cave floor. After that I had the others draw lots: which of them would dare to lift the stake with me and grind it into the giant's eye when sweet sleep had taken him. The lot fell on the very four I would have chosen, and I made a fifth. That evening he came back driving his fleecy flocks, and this time he brought the whole flock in, leaving none in the deep yard outside — whether some thought struck him, or a god put it in his mind. He heaved the great stone up and set it in the doorway, then sat and milked his ewes and bleating goats, each in turn, and set her young one under each. When he had finished his work in haste, again he seized two of my men and made his supper of them. And then I came up close to the Cyclops, holding out an ivy-wood bowl brimful of the dark wine, and said:

"'Here, Cyclops, drink some wine, now that you have feasted on the flesh of men, and learn what kind of vintage our ship was carrying. I was bringing it as an offering to you, hoping you might pity me and send me on my way home. But your savagery is past all bearing. You hard heart — how can you think any other man on earth will ever come to you again, when you do such lawless things?'

"He took it and drank it off, and the sweet drink delighted him so much that he begged me for another bowl. 'Be a good fellow and give me more,' he said, 'and tell me your name, here and now, so that I may give you a guest-gift to make your heart glad. Our own rich soil bears the Cyclopes wine, too, from great clusters that the rain of Zeus swells full; but this is a draught of pure nectar and ambrosia.'

"So I filled the bowl for him again. Three times I poured it, and three times the fool drank it down. And when at last the wine had clouded his wits, I spoke to him in soft and winning words: 'Cyclops, you ask my honored name, and I will tell it — and you give me the guest-gift you promised. Nobody is my name. Nobody my mother and father call me, and all my friends.'
"And the cruel creature answered me at once: 'Then Nobody I will eat last of all his company, and the others first. That is the gift I give you.'

"As he spoke he toppled backward and fell sprawling on his back, his thick neck lolling sideways, and sleep, the tamer of all, came over him. Out of his gullet poured wine and gobbets of human flesh, for the drink had heaved him up. Then I drove the stake deep under the ashes to heat it, and put heart into my men with steadying words, so that not one would shrink back in fear. When the olive stake, green as it was, was on the very point of catching fire and glowing terribly, I drew it from the embers, and my men stood close around me, and a god breathed great courage into us all. They took the sharpened olive stake and drove it into his eye, while I leaned my weight on it from above and turned it — the way a man bores a ship's timber with a drill, while the others below keep it spinning with a strap, and the drill runs on and on without stopping. So we took the fire-pointed stake and spun it in his eye, and the blood came boiling up around the burning point. The searing heat of the eyeball singed off all his brows and lashes, and the roots of the eye crackled in the flame. As a smith plunges a great axe or an adze into cold water and it shrieks aloud — for that is the secret of the iron's strength — so his eye hissed around the olive stake. He let out a hideous howl, and the rock walls rang with it, and we shrank back in terror. He wrenched the stake from his eye, all fouled and slick with blood, and hurled it from him, flailing his arms, and bellowed to the other Cyclopes who lived around him in their caves along the windy heights. They heard his cry and came crowding from every side to stand about his cave, and called out, asking what was wrong:

"'Polyphemus, what is it? Why such a terrible cry in the still of the holy night, robbing us of our sleep? Surely no man is driving off your flocks against your will? Surely no man is killing you, by trickery or by force?'
"And from inside the cave mighty Polyphemus called back to them: 'My friends — Nobody is killing me, by trickery, not by force!'

"And their winged answer came: 'Well, if nobody is doing you violence, and you are all alone, there is no help for the sickness that great Zeus sends a man — pray, then, to your father, Lord Poseidon.'

"With that they went off, and the heart in me laughed to think how my name and my flawless cunning had fooled them. But the Cyclops, groaning and writhing in his pain, groped along the wall with his hands until he found the stone and dragged it from the doorway, and then sat himself down in the entrance with his arms spread wide, to catch anyone trying to slip out among the sheep — for he must have thought me fool enough to try it that way.

"But I was turning over plan after plan, searching for the one that would save the lives of my men and my own; for death stood close, and the danger was great. And of them all, this was the plan I judged the best. The rams were broad and well grown, with thick fleeces of dark wool. These I lashed together silently in threes, with the twisted withies the lawless monster slept on; the middle ram of each three would carry a man, and the two on either side would walk beside him and shield him. So three rams bore each man across. For myself, there was one ram, far the finest of the whole flock; I gripped him by the back, swung myself in under his shaggy belly, and lay there face up, both hands twisted tight in the marvelous fleece, holding on with a steady heart. So, sighing, we waited for the holy dawn.

"When the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn, appeared, the rams went butting out to pasture, while the unmilked ewes bleated about the pens, their udders near to bursting. Their master, racked with pain, ran his hands along the backs of all the rams as they passed him standing upright — never guessing, the fool, that my men were lashed beneath the woolly bellies. Last of all the great ram went to the door, heavy with his own fleece and with the weight of me and my scheming. And mighty Polyphemus laid his hands on him and said:

"'My good ram, why are you the last of all the flock to leave the cave? You were never one to lag behind the others. No, you would always be first, striding out ahead to graze the soft grass and the running streams, first to reach the fold again at evening — and now you come last of all. Is it that you grieve for your master's eye, which a vile man and his wretched crew have put out, after they fuddled my wits with wine — Nobody, who has not yet escaped his death, I swear it! If only you could think and speak like me, and tell me where he is skulking from my rage, I would dash his brains across the floor of the cave and ease the misery this good-for-nothing Nobody has brought on me.'

"With that he sent the ram out through the door. When we had got a little way from the cave and the yard, I first slipped out from under the ram, and then untied my men. And quickly, often glancing back, we drove the long-shanked, fat-thighed sheep down to the ship. My dear companions were glad indeed to see us — those of us who had escaped death — but they broke into weeping and wailing for the rest. I would not let them: I frowned and shook my head at each of them to silence their grief, and ordered them to fling the fine fleecy sheep aboard at once and put out over the salt sea. They climbed in, took their places, and beat the grey sea white with their oars. But when I was as far off as a man's shout will carry, I called back to the Cyclops, taunting him:

"'Cyclops! So he was no weakling after all, the man whose comrades you murdered and ate in your hollow cave! Your evil deeds were bound to fall back on your own head, you brute, who had no shame to devour your own guests in your own house. Now Zeus and the other gods have paid you out.'

"That set him blazing with fury. He tore loose the peak of a great mountain and flung it, and it crashed down just ahead of the dark-prowed ship, barely clearing the steering-oar's tip. The sea heaved up where the rock plunged in, and the backwash of the swell drove us in toward the land again, the wave sweeping us hard against the shore. But I caught up a long pole and shoved us off, and with a jerk of my head I signaled the crew to throw their backs into the oars and save their lives; and they bent to it with a will. When we had pulled out twice as far as before, I was ready to taunt the Cyclops again, but the men crowded round me on every side, begging me to stop:

"'Are you mad? Why provoke this wild thing further? Already the rock he hurled into the sea drove the ship back to land, and we were sure we were finished. If he hears so much as a sound from one of us, he will let fly another jagged crag and smash our heads and the ship's timbers to pulp — his throw carries that far.'

"But they could not bend my stubborn heart, and I shouted back at him a second time, in my anger: 'Cyclops, if ever any mortal man asks you who put out your eye and shamed you, tell him it was Odysseus, sacker of cities, the son of Laertes, whose home is in Ithaca!'

"At that he gave a great groan and cried out: 'No — so the old prophecy has come home to me at last! There was a seer here once, a tall and noble man, Telemus son of Eurymus, the best of prophets, who grew old foretelling among the Cyclopes. He told me all this would come to pass in time — that I would lose my sight at the hands of one called Odysseus. But I always looked for some tall and handsome man to come, armed in great strength. And now a little nothing of a man, a feeble weakling, has blinded my eye — but only after he downed me with his wine. Come back, Odysseus, and let me give you the gifts a guest is owed, and beg the great Earth-Shaker to send you safely home. For I am his son, and he calls himself my father. He, if he wishes — and no other, neither god nor man — can heal me.'

"And I answered him: 'I only wish I could be as certain of robbing you of your life and your breath and sending you down to the house of Hades, as I am that not even the Earth-Shaker will ever heal that eye of yours.'

"At that he stretched out his hands toward the starry sky and prayed to Lord Poseidon: 'Hear me, Poseidon, dark-haired holder of the earth. If I am truly yours, and you are truly my father, grant that Odysseus, sacker of cities, the son of Laertes, who has his home in Ithaca, never reaches his home again. But if it is his fate to see his own people and come back to his high-roofed house and his native land, then let him come late, and broken, having lost every last one of his companions, in a ship that is not his own — and let him find nothing but trouble in his house.'

"So he prayed, and the dark-haired god heard him. Then the Cyclops heaved up a stone far greater than the first, swung it, and hurled it with measureless force. It fell just astern of the dark-prowed ship, barely missing the tip of the steering-oar. The sea heaved up where the rock plunged in, and the wave drove us forward, sweeping us on toward the far island.

"And so we came back to the island where the rest of our well-benched ships lay waiting all together, and our companions sat around them, grieving, watching the sea for us. We ran the ship up onto the sand and waded ashore, and unloaded the Cyclops's flocks from the deep hull and shared them out, so fairly that no man went without his portion. As for the great ram, when the sheep were divided my dear companions gave him to me alone, beyond my share; and there on the beach I sacrificed him to Zeus, the dark-clouded son of Kronos, who is lord of all, and burned the thigh-pieces in his honor. But he took no heed of my offering; even then he was laying his plans to destroy all my well-benched ships and my faithful men.

"So all that long day, until the sun went down, we sat and feasted on the rich meat and the sweet wine. And when the sun had set and darkness came on, we lay down to sleep along the breaking surf. Then, when the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn, appeared, I roused my men and ordered them aboard to cast off the cables. They climbed in, took their places, and beat the grey sea white with their oars. So we sailed on, sick at heart, glad to be alive but grieving for the dear companions we had lost."
books.title: The Cicones, the Lotus-Eaters, and the Cyclops

books.label: Book X
paragraphs: From there we came to the island of Aeolia, where Aeolus lived, the son of Hippotas, dear to the immortal gods. It is a floating island, ringed all around with a wall of unbreakable bronze, and the rock of it rises sheer out of the sea. Aeolus has twelve children inside that hall — six daughters and six sons, all grown — and he gave his daughters to his sons to be their wives. They live beside their dear father and their gentle mother, with feasting laid before them that never ends. All day long the house is thick with the smell of roasting meat, and the courtyard rings with it; and at night each of them sleeps beside his own wife, on a bed spread with blankets, in the well-made hall. These were the people we had come among.

Aeolus welcomed me as a guest and kept me a full month, asking me about everything — Troy, the Greek ships, how we sailed for home. I told him the whole of it, just as it happened. And when at last I asked him to send me on my way, he made no difficulty; he set about it gladly. He flayed the hide of a nine-year-old ox and made it into a bag, and into that bag he bound the ways of the howling winds — for Zeus had made him the winds' keeper, to rouse them or still them as he pleased. He stowed the bag in the hold of my ship and lashed its mouth shut with a bright silver cord, so that not even a breath could slip out from any side. The one wind he left free was the West Wind, to blow us home. But it came to nothing in the end — and the ruin we brought down was our own.

Nine days we sailed, nine days and nights together, and on the tenth our own land at last came up over the water — so near that we could see men tending their watch-fires along the shore. And just then, dead-tired, I fell asleep. I had held the steering-oar myself the whole way, never trusting it to any of the men, so we might come home the faster. But while I slept the crew began to talk among themselves. They had it that I was carrying gold and silver home in the bag, the gift of great-hearted Aeolus, and one would turn to the man beside him and say: "It's a wonder, the way everyone loves this man and heaps him with honor, whatever land he comes to. Look at the fine plunder he's bringing back from Troy — and the rest of us, who came every weary mile he did, going home empty-handed. And now Aeolus has loaded him with all this on top of it, out of pure friendship. Come — quick — let's see what's in it. How much gold and silver is tied up in that bag?"

That was the talk, and the bad counsel won. They opened the bag — and out roared every wind at once. The storm caught us and swept us back out to sea, away from home, the men weeping. I woke to it, and for a moment I weighed in my heart whether to go over the side and drown then and there, or hold on and bear it and stay among the living. I held on. I bore it. I wrapped myself in my cloak and lay down in the ship while the wild gale carried the whole fleet back, my men groaning, all the way to the island of Aeolus.

We went ashore and drew fresh water, and the men ate their meal there by the ships. When we had eaten, I took one herald and one of the crew and went straight up to the house of Aeolus — and there I found him at the feast, with his wife and his children. We came in and sat down as suppliants on the threshold, by the doorpost, and they stared at us, astonished. "Odysseus — how is this?" they said. "What god has set himself against you? We sent you off with such care, to bring you home to Ithaca, or wherever in the world you wished to go."
That is what they said, and I answered, sick at heart: "My own crew undid me — they and a cruel sleep. Make it good for me, my friends; you have the power, if you will."

I pleaded as gently as I could, but they sat in silence. Only their father answered, and his words were hard: "Off this island — now — you lowest thing alive. It is not for me to take in and send onward a man the blessed gods hate. Get out. You come here cursed by heaven." And with that he drove me from his door, and I went grieving.

From there we sailed on, heavy at heart. The spirit went out of the men at the oars, worn down by the cruel rowing, for now there was no wind at all to help them, and the fault was our own folly. Six days we toiled, days and nights together, and on the seventh we came to the high citadel of Lamus — to Telepylus, the city of the Laestrygonians. It is a strange country: there the night and the day run so close together that a herdsman driving his flocks in at dusk calls out to a herdsman driving his out, and that one calls back. A man who could go without sleep might earn double wages there — one for keeping the cattle, one for pasturing the white sheep — for the paths of the night and the day lie near each other.

We came into a fine harbor, ringed all around by sheer cliffs, with two headlands running out to make a narrow mouth between them. There my captains brought all their ships inside and moored them close together, gunwale to gunwale, for inside that water no wave ever rose, great or small; it lay always dead calm. But I alone kept my black ship outside, at the very point, and made her fast to the rock there. Then I climbed a high crag to look around. I could see no plowed field, no cattle, no sign of men — only smoke going up from somewhere over the land. So I sent two of my men, with a third to go with them, to find out who lived in that country.

They went ashore and followed a smooth road, the one the wagons take, hauling timber down from the high hills into the town. Outside the walls they met a girl drawing water — the tall daughter of Antiphates the Laestrygonian. She had come down to the clear spring of Artacia, where the people fetch their water, and the men went up and asked her who was king here, and over what people he ruled. She pointed them at once to her father's high-roofed house. But when they went in they found his wife — a woman huge as a mountain peak — and the sight of her froze their blood.

Straightaway she shouted for her husband, Antiphates, from the meeting-place, and he came, and his welcome was death. He snatched up one of my men on the spot and made his meal of him. The other two sprang up and ran for their lives, back to the ships — but Antiphates raised the alarm through the town, and the mighty Laestrygonians came running from every side, thousands of them, more like giants than men. They tore great boulders from the cliffs, each the load of a man, and hurled them down on us; and there rose up from the ships a horrible din — timbers splintering, men dying — as the giants speared them like fish and carried them off to make their grim feast. While they were killing my men there in the deep harbor, I drew the sharp sword from my thigh, slashed through the cables of my dark-prowed ship, and shouted to my own crew to throw their backs into the oars and pull, if they wanted to live. In terror of death they pulled as one, and my ship leapt clear of the overhanging rocks, out to open water. But all the rest were lost there together — every one.

On from there we sailed, grieving in our hearts, glad to be alive and yet sick for the friends we had lost. And we came to the island of Aeaea, where Circe lived — Circe of the lovely braids, a dread goddess with a human voice, own sister to Aeetes, the wizard whose mind runs to ruin. Both of them were children of Helios, who gives light to mortals, born to him by Perse, the daughter of Ocean. There we brought our ship in to the shore without a sound, into a sheltered cove — some god was guiding us. We landed, and for two days and two nights we lay where we were, worn out in body and worn out in spirit, eating our hearts with grief.

But when fair-haired Dawn brought up the third morning, I took my spear and my keen sword and climbed up from the ship to a high lookout, hoping to catch some sign of men at work, or the sound of voices. And standing on that rocky height I saw it — smoke going up from Circe's house, far off through the dense scrub and the forest. I turned it over in my mind, whether to go straight on and learn more, now that I had seen the smoke. And in the end it seemed the better course to go back down to the ship and the shore, give the men their meal, and send a party to find out, rather than go alone.

On my way down, near the ship, some god took pity on me there in my loneliness, and sent a great stag with towering antlers right across my path. The heat of the noon had driven him down out of the woodland pasture to drink at the river, and as he came I struck him square in the spine, and the bronze point drove clean through, and he dropped in the dust with a bellow, and his life flew out of him. I set my foot on him, pulled the spear from the wound, and laid it on the ground; then I gathered twigs and willow shoots and twisted a good rope, a fathom long, and lashed the great beast's four feet together. I slung him round my neck and carried him down to the ship, leaning on the spear, for he was far too big to balance on one shoulder with a hand — he was an enormous creature. I threw him down in front of the ship and roused the men with cheerful words, going from one to the next: "Friends — beaten as we are, we are not going down to the house of Hades before our day. Not while there's meat and drink still in the ship. Up, now — let's not waste away with hunger."

At that they took heart. They threw off their cloaks there on the shore and stood marveling at the stag, for he was a splendid thing. And when they had feasted their eyes, they washed their hands and set about a glad feast. So all that day, till the sun went down, we sat there filling ourselves with meat past counting and sweet wine; and when the sun set and the dark came on, we slept by the breaking surf. But when rosy-fingered Dawn appeared, the child of morning, I called them all together and spoke to them: "Friends — listen to me, hard as things stand. We have no idea, men, where the darkness lies or where the dawn, where the sun goes down to the world below or where it climbs again. Let us think, while there's still time, whether there's any way out — and I can see none. I climbed to a rocky height and looked: this is an island, low-lying, with the endless sea drawn round it like a ring. And in the middle of it I saw smoke, going up through the thick woods."

At that their hearts broke in them. They remembered everything — Antiphates the Laestrygonian, and the savage, lawless Cyclops — and they wept aloud, the great tears falling. But there was nothing to be won by crying. So I counted them off into two companies and set a leader over each: one I took myself, and the other I gave to godlike Eurylochus. Then we shook the lots in a bronze helmet, and out jumped the lot of brave Eurylochus. So off he went, weeping, and with him twenty-two of the men — and the rest of us were left behind, weeping too.

Deep in the glens they came on Circe's house, built of dressed stone on open, commanding ground. All around it prowled wolves of the mountain and lions — creatures she herself had bewitched, drugging them with her wicked potions. They did not set upon the men; they came up, fawning, wagging their long tails, the way dogs crowd around their master when he comes home from a feast, for he always has some good thing for them in his hands. Just so those great-clawed wolves and lions fawned about my men — and the men were terrified, face to face with such monsters. They stopped in the gateway of the lovely-haired goddess, and from inside they could hear Circe singing in a beautiful voice as she worked at her great loom, weaving a web wide and shimmering and delicate, the kind of fine, radiant work that only the hands of a goddess make. Polites spoke up first — a leader of men, and dearest to me, the one I trusted most: "Friends, someone inside is working a great loom and singing — beautifully — and the whole place rings with it. Goddess or woman, let's call out to her."

So they called, and she came. She opened the bright doors and asked them in, and they all followed her, knowing no better — all but Eurylochus, who hung back, suspecting a trap. She led them in and seated them on chairs and benches, and stirred up for them a brew of cheese and barley meal and pale honey in Pramnian wine — but into the food she mixed her cruel drugs, to wipe their homeland clean out of their minds. When they had drunk it down, she struck them with her wand and herded them into the pens of her pigsty. They had the heads of pigs now, the bristles, the grunting, the whole shape of them — but the mind inside was still a man's, unchanged. So they were penned, weeping, while Circe threw them acorns and beechmast and the red cornel-berries, the food of pigs that wallow in the mud.

Eurylochus ran straight back to the swift black ship to bring word of his comrades and their bitter fate. But for all his trying he could not get a word out — the grief had struck him dumb, his eyes brimming, his heart set only on weeping. We pressed him with questions, every one of us amazed, until at last he found his voice and told us how the others were lost: "We went off through the oak woods, brilliant Odysseus, as you ordered, and deep in the glens we found a fine house of dressed stone, on open ground. Someone was inside, working a great loom and singing in a clear, high voice — a goddess, or a woman — and the men called out to her. She came at once, opened the shining doors, and asked them in, and the whole crowd of them followed her, knowing no better. But I stayed where I was; I smelled a trap. And every one of them vanished. Not one came out again, though I sat a long, long time and watched."

When I heard that, I slung my great bronze-studded sword across my shoulders, took up my bow, and told Eurylochus to lead me back the way he had come. But he threw both arms around my knees and begged me, the words pouring out of him: "Don't make me go back there, my lord — leave me here. I know it: you'll never come back yourself, and you'll never bring one of the others with you. Let's get away, the rest of us, now, while we can. We may still save our lives."

And I said to him: "Eurylochus — then stay here yourself, eating and drinking beside the black ship. But I am going. There is a hard necessity laid on me." And with that I left the ship and the sea behind me and went up inland.

I had come through the sacred glens and was near the great house of Circe, the witch of many drugs, when Hermes met me — Hermes of the golden wand — in the very road. He had the look of a young man with the first down on his lip, in the fairest bloom of his youth. He took me by the hand and spoke my name: "Where are you off to now, you luckless man, alone, over these hills, in a country you don't know? Your men are penned in Circe's sty, over there, shut up like swine in their close pens. Have you come to set them free? I tell you, you won't get away yourself — you'll stay there with the rest. But never mind. I'll save you from it; I'll bring you through. Here — take this herb, a good one, and keep it on you when you go to Circe's house, and it will turn the day of ruin from your head.

"Now I'll tell you every trick of Circe's deadly craft. She'll mix you a brew, and slip her drugs into the food — but she won't be able to charm you, for this good herb I'm giving you won't let her. Here is what to do. The moment Circe strikes you with her long wand, draw the sharp sword from your thigh and rush at her as if you meant to run her through. She'll shrink back in terror and ask you into her bed — and you must not refuse a goddess's bed, not if you want her to free your men and take care of you. But make her swear first the great oath of the blessed gods that she'll plot no new harm against you — or else, once she has you stripped, she'll unman you and leave you good for nothing."

And as he spoke, the slayer of Argos pulled the herb out of the ground and showed me what it was. Its root was black, but the flower was white as milk. The gods call it moly. It is hard for mortal men to dig — but the gods can do anything. Then Hermes was gone, away over the wooded island, back toward high Olympus, and I went on to the house of Circe, and my heart was dark with many thoughts as I walked.

I stood at the gates of the lovely-haired goddess and called, and she heard me and came at once, opened the bright doors, and asked me in; and I followed, sick at heart. She brought me to a beautiful chair, silver-studded, with a footstool under my feet, and mixed me a brew in a golden cup to drink — and into it she slipped her drug, for her mind was set on harm. She gave it to me, and I drank, and it did not charm me. Then she struck me with her wand and said, "Off to the sty now — go wallow with the rest of your friends." But I drew the sharp sword from my thigh and rushed at her as if to kill her, and she gave a great scream and ducked under the blade and caught me by the knees, and the words came pouring out: "Who are you? Where do you come from — what city, what people? It is a marvel: you drank my drugs and they did not charm you, and no other man alive has ever withstood them, once they passed his lips. There is a mind in you no spell can touch. You must be Odysseus, the man of many turns — the one Hermes of the golden wand always told me would come here, on his way home from Troy in his swift black ship. Come, then — sheathe your sword. Let us two go up into my bed, and lie together, and learn to trust each other there."

But I answered her: "Circe — how can you ask me to be gentle with you, when in this very hall you have turned my men into swine? And now you have me here, and your mind is set on treachery, asking me to your bed, so that once you have me stripped you can unman me and leave me nothing. No — I will not go up into your bed unless you bring yourself to swear me a great oath, goddess, that you'll plot no new harm against me." So I spoke, and at once she swore the oath I asked. And when she had sworn it and the oath was done, then I went up into the beautiful bed of Circe.

Meanwhile her four handmaids were at their work about the hall — the spirits of the springs and the woodland groves and the sacred rivers that run down to the sea. One spread the chairs with fine purple cloths and laid a smooth carpet beneath. Another drew up silver tables before them and set out baskets of gold. A third mixed sweet wine with water in a silver bowl and ranged the golden cups. And the fourth carried in water and lit a great fire beneath a tall cauldron until the water grew hot. When it sang in the gleaming bronze, she set me in the bath and washed me, easing the soul-deep weariness out of my limbs with water tempered to my liking, pouring it over my head and shoulders. And when she had bathed me and rubbed me with rich oil, she dressed me in a fine cloak and tunic and led me to a chair, a beautiful one, silver-studded, with a footstool for my feet. A maid brought water in a lovely golden pitcher and poured it over my hands into a silver basin, and drew a polished table up beside me. A grave housekeeper set out bread and many good things, and pressed me to eat. But I had no heart for it. I sat with my mind elsewhere, brooding, sensing trouble still.

When Circe saw me sitting there, not reaching for the food, deep in my grief, she came close and spoke winged words: "Odysseus, why do you sit like this, like a man struck dumb, eating your own heart and touching neither food nor drink? Do you still think I mean some treachery? You have no cause to fear. I have already sworn you the great oath."

And I answered her: "Circe — what man with any sense of right could bring himself to eat or drink before he had seen his comrades free, here, with his own eyes? If you truly mean me well, set them loose. Let me see my faithful friends." So I spoke, and Circe walked out through the hall with her wand in her hand, opened the doors of the sty, and drove them out — and they came, in the likeness of nine-year hogs. They stood there facing her, and she went down the line and rubbed each one with another drug, and the bristles the first vile potion had grown dropped away, and they were men again — younger than before, and taller, and finer to look at. They knew me, and each one caught my hand, and such a sweet weeping rose among them that the whole house rang with it; and even the goddess was moved. She came and stood beside me and said: "Odysseus, son of Laertes, born of the gods — go down now to your swift ship and the sea. First haul the ship up onto the dry land, and stow all your gear and your cargo away in the caves. Then come back here, and bring your faithful comrades with you."

I agreed, and went down to the swift ship and the shore, and there I found the men by the ship, grieving, the tears running down. The way calves around the farmyard come bounding to meet the cows when they trail home full-fed to the pen — leaping, mooing, the byres ringing, the fences no longer able to hold them — so my men, the moment they laid eyes on me, came crowding round me weeping; and to their hearts it felt as if they had come home, home to rugged Ithaca, to the very town where they were born and raised. And through their tears they cried out: "You're back — and to us, brilliant Odysseus, it's as if we'd reached Ithaca, our own land. But tell us — how did the rest of our company die?"

I spoke to them gently: "First let's drag the ship up onto the land, and stow our gear and all our cargo in the caves. Then come with me, all of you, and you'll see your comrades in Circe's holy halls, eating and drinking with plenty before them." At that they were ready to come at once — all but Eurylochus, who tried to hold them back, and his words were urgent: "Where are we rushing, you poor fools? Why are we so hungry for our own ruin — going down to Circe's house, where she'll turn the lot of us into pigs, or wolves, or lions, and pen us to guard her great hall by force? It will be just like the Cyclops, when our friends went into that cave, and this same reckless Odysseus led them — it was his folly that got them killed."

When I heard that, I half drew the long sword from beside my thigh, ready to strike his head off and roll it in the dust, close kin of mine though he was by marriage. But the men crowded round and held me back, every one of them pleading: "Born of the gods — let this man stay behind, if you will, to guard the ship. But lead the rest of us to Circe's holy house." So they spoke, and went up from the ship and the sea. And Eurylochus did not stay behind by the ship after all; he came along too, cowed by the hard edge in my voice.

Meanwhile Circe had been taking kind care of the others, back at her hall. She had them bathed and rubbed with oil, dressed in soft fleecy cloaks and tunics; and we found them all at the feast, in good comfort. When the men saw one another face to face and knew each other, they wept for joy until the whole house echoed with it. Then the lovely goddess came up to me and said: "Odysseus, son of Laertes, born of the gods — no more of this weeping now. I know it myself, all you have suffered on the teeming sea, all the harm cruel men did you ashore. Come — eat, drink, until the spirit rises again in your chests, the spirit you had when you first sailed from your own land, from rugged Ithaca. As it is, you are worn thin and faint of heart, your minds always on the bitterness of your wandering; there is no joy left in you, for you have suffered so much."

So she spoke, and our proud hearts said yes. And there we stayed, day after day, a whole year round, feasting on meat past counting and sweet wine. But when the year had turned full circle — the seasons coming round, the moons waning away, the long days running out — then my faithful men called me aside and said: "My lord — it is time, at last, to remember your own country, if it is fated you should be saved and reach your high-roofed house and the land of your fathers."

So they spoke, and my proud heart agreed. So all that day, until the sun went down, we sat feasting on meat past counting and sweet wine; and when the sun had set and the dark came on, the men lay down to sleep through the shadowy halls. But I climbed into Circe's lovely bed, and clasped her knees, and the goddess heard me out as I begged her: "Circe — keep now the promise you made me, to send me home. My heart is set on it, and so are my men's; they wear me down with their grieving, whenever you are out of earshot."

And the lovely goddess answered me at once: "Odysseus, son of Laertes, born of the gods — you shall not stay on in my house against your will. But there is another journey you must make first. You have to go down to the house of Hades and dread Persephone, to consult the ghost of Tiresias of Thebes, the blind seer, whose mind is sound even in death. To him alone, dead as he is, Persephone has left his wits whole; the other shades go flitting about like shadows."

When I heard that, the heart broke in me. I sat there on the bed and wept; I had no more wish to live, no wish to see the light of the sun. But when I had wept and writhed my fill, I said to her: "Circe — who is to guide me on that road? No man has ever yet reached the house of Hades in a black ship."

And the lovely goddess answered me at once: "You will need no guide. Step the mast, spread the white sail, and sit still; the breath of the North Wind will carry you there of itself. When your ship has crossed the stream of Ocean, you will come to a low shore and the groves of Persephone — tall poplars, and willows that drop their fruit unripe. Beach your ship there, by the deep eddies of Ocean, and go on yourself to the moldering house of Hades. There the river Pyriphlegethon and the Cocytus, which is an arm of the water of the Styx, run into Acheron, and there is a rock where the two roaring rivers meet.

"Go up close to that, hero — listen well — and dig a pit, a forearm's length each way, and pour around it an offering to all the dead: first honey mixed with milk, then sweet wine, and the third time water, and scatter white barley meal over it all. Pray hard to the strengthless heads of the dead, and vow that when you reach Ithaca you will sacrifice a barren heifer, your best, in your halls, and heap the fire with good things; and to Tiresias alone, apart, vow a black ram, the finest in your flocks. When you have prayed to the famous nations of the dead, then sacrifice a ram and a black ewe, turning their heads down toward Erebus while you yourself look away, back toward the streams of the river. Then the souls of the dead and gone will come thronging up. Call to your men, and have them flay and burn the sheep that lie there killed by the pitiless bronze, with prayers to the gods — to mighty Hades and dread Persephone. And you yourself, draw the sharp sword from your thigh and sit there, and do not let the strengthless heads of the dead come near the blood until you have asked Tiresias all you would know. The seer will come to you soon, leader of men, and he will tell you the way and the measure of your road, and how you are to make your passage home over the teeming sea."

She had hardly finished when golden Dawn came up. Circe dressed me in cloak and tunic, and threw about herself a long silvery robe, fine and graceful, and clasped a beautiful golden belt at her waist, and veiled her head. Then I went through the hall and roused the men, standing over each one with gentle words: "No more sweet sleep now. Up — we are going. Lady Circe has told me the whole of it." And their proud hearts agreed.

Yet even then I did not lead them all away unharmed. There was one of us, Elpenor — the youngest of all, no great fighter, and none too steady in his wits. He had wandered off to sleep apart from the rest, up on the flat roof of Circe's house, looking for the cool, heavy with wine. He heard the noise and the bustle of the men setting out, and started up all at once, and clean forgot to go back down by the long ladder. He pitched headlong from the roof, and his neck snapped at the spine, and his soul went down to the house of Hades.

When the rest were gathered, I spoke to them: "You think, no doubt, that we are bound now for home, for our own dear country. But Circe has set us another road — down to the house of Hades and dread Persephone, to consult the ghost of Tiresias of Thebes." At that the heart broke in them; they sank down where they stood, groaning, and tore their hair. But no good came of their grieving. And as we made our way down to the swift ship and the shore, weeping, the great tears falling, Circe had gone on ahead and tethered a ram and a black ewe close by the ship — slipping past us easily, unseen. For who can lay eyes on a god going to and fro, when the god does not wish to be seen?
books.title: Aeolus, the Laestrygonians, and Circe

books.label: Book XI
paragraphs: "When we had come down to the sea and the ship, the first thing we did was drag her into the bright water and step the mast and set the sails. Then we took the sheep and put them aboard, and climbed in ourselves, heartsick and weeping. And Circe, that dread goddess with a human voice, sent us a good companion behind the dark-prowed ship — a fair wind that filled the sail and held steady, so that we had nothing to do but sit while the wind and the helmsman kept her straight. All day long the sail strained as she ran on across the open sea, until the sun went down and all the roads of the world grew dark.

"So we came to the deep-running stream of Ocean, the river that circles the edge of the world, and to the land and the city of the Cimmerians, a people wrapped forever in mist and cloud. The bright sun never looks down on them with his rays — not when he climbs into the starry sky, not when he turns again from heaven toward the earth — but a deadly night is stretched over those wretched people without end. There we ran the ship aground and put the sheep ashore, and walked along the stream of Ocean until we reached the place Circe had named.

"There Perimedes and Eurylochus held the victims fast, while I drew the sharp sword from my thigh and dug a pit, a forearm's length each way. Around it I poured an offering to all the dead — first with milk and honey, then with sweet wine, and a third time with water — and over it I scattered white barley. And I prayed long to the strengthless heads of the dead, vowing that when I came home to Ithaca I would sacrifice my best barren heifer in my own halls and heap the fire with rich gifts; and to Tiresias alone I promised, apart, a ram all black, the finest in my flocks. When I had prayed and made my vows to the great company of the dead, I took the two sheep and cut their throats over the pit, and the dark blood ran down.

"Then up out of Erebus they came swarming, the spirits of the dead and gone — brides and unmarried boys and old men worn down by their long labor; tender girls with grief still fresh in their hearts; and many men cut down in battle, run through by bronze spears, their armor still dark with blood. From every side they crowded the pit with an eerie crying, and a pale terror took hold of me. But I called to my men and told them to flay the sheep that lay there killed by the pitiless bronze, and burn them, and pray to the gods — to mighty Hades and to dread Persephone. And I myself sat with my drawn sword and would not let the powerless ghosts come near the blood until I had questioned Tiresias.

"The first to come was the spirit of my comrade Elpenor. We had not yet buried him under the wide earth; we had left his body behind us in Circe's hall, unwept and unburied, because other work pressed hard on us. I wept when I saw him, and pity took hold of me, and I spoke to him, my words flying: 'Elpenor, how did you come down here into the gloom and the dark? You came faster on foot than I did in my black ship.'

"And he answered me with a groan: 'Royal son of Laertes, Odysseus of the many turns — a god's cruel doom undid me, and too much wine. I had bedded down on Circe's roof, and never thought to climb down again by the long ladder. I fell headlong; my neck snapped at the spine, and my soul went down to the house of Hades. Now I beg you, by those you left behind, by your wife, by the father who raised you when you were small, and by Telemachus, the only son you left in your halls — for I know that when you leave this place you will put in again at the island of Aeaea with your trim ship — there, my lord, remember me. Do not sail off and leave me unwept and unburied, or I may become a cause of the gods' anger against you. Burn me with all the armor that is mine, and heap me a mound on the shore of the grey sea, so men in the days to come will know my sorry story. Do this for me — and fix upon my grave the oar I pulled at while I lived, when I rowed among my friends.'

"And I answered him: 'All this, poor friend, I will do. I will not fail you.' So we two sat there trading our sad words — I on the one side, holding my sword out over the blood, and the ghost of my comrade speaking on from the other.

"Then came the spirit of my own dead mother, Anticleia, the daughter of great-hearted Autolycus. I had left her living when I sailed for sacred Troy. I wept to see her, and pity went through me — but even in all my grief, I would not let her come near the blood before I had questioned Tiresias.

"Then came the spirit of Theban Tiresias, his golden staff in his hand. He knew me and spoke: 'Royal son of Laertes, Odysseus of the many turns — why have you come, you luckless man, leaving the light of the sun to look on the dead and this joyless place? Stand back from the pit and lower your sharp sword, so I may drink the blood and tell you the truth.'
"So I drew back and slid the silver-studded sword into its sheath. And when he had drunk the dark blood, the faultless prophet spoke to me at last.

"'You are searching for your sweet homecoming, glorious Odysseus,' he said, 'but a god will make it hard. For I do not think you will slip past the Earthshaker, who has set his heart in anger against you, enraged that you blinded his dear son. Even so, you and your men may still come home, for all your suffering — if you can master your own hunger and theirs when first your ship touches the island of Thrinacia, your escape from the violet sea. For there you will find grazing the cattle and the fat flocks of Helios the Sun, who sees all things and hears all things. Leave them unharmed, keep your mind fixed on your homecoming, and you may yet reach Ithaca, hard as the road will be. But if you harm them, then I foretell ruin — for your ship and for your men. And even if you save yourself, you will come home late and broken, having lost all your companions, in a stranger's ship — and you will find trouble waiting in your house: insolent men devouring your goods, courting your godlike wife, pressing their gifts on her.

"'But you will make those men pay for their outrages when you come. And after you have killed the suitors in your halls — by cunning or in the open, by the sharp bronze — then you must go out again. Take a well-cut oar and carry it on your shoulder until you come to men who know nothing of the sea, who eat their food unsalted, who have never seen ships with their painted cheeks or the oars that are the wings of a ship. And I will give you a sign so clear you cannot miss it. When another traveler, meeting you, says you have a winnowing-fan on your strong shoulder — then plant your oar in the ground and make fine offerings to lord Poseidon: a ram, a bull, and a boar that mounts the sows. Then go home and offer sacred hecatombs to the deathless gods who hold the wide heavens, to all of them, each in his turn. And death will come to you, far from the sea — a gentle death that will take you down when you are worn out in a sleek old age, your people prospering around you. All this I tell you is the truth.'

"And I answered him: 'Tiresias, surely the gods themselves have spun this out as my fate. But tell me this, and tell me true. I see the spirit of my dead mother here. She sits near the blood in silence, and cannot bring herself to look her own son in the face or say a word to him. Tell me, my lord — how can I make her know me for who I am?'

"And he answered me at once: 'That is an easy thing to tell you. Whichever of the dead you let come near the blood will speak to you, and speak the truth. But the one you refuse will turn and go back again.' And with that the spirit of lord Tiresias went back into the house of Hades, his prophecy spoken.

"But I stayed where I was until my mother came up and drank the dark blood. At once she knew me, and her grief broke into words: 'My child, how did you come down here, into all this darkness, and you still alive? It is hard for the living to look on these things. Between us and you lie great rivers and dreadful waters — Ocean first of all, which no man can cross on foot, but only in a well-built ship. Have you come here from Troy, wandering all this long while with your ship and your men? Have you not yet reached Ithaca, not yet seen your wife in your own halls?'

"And I answered her: 'Mother, I had no choice — I had to come down to the house of Hades to ask the spirit of Theban Tiresias. I have not yet come near Greece, not yet set foot on my own soil. I have been wandering in misery from the first day I followed great Agamemnon to Ilios, the land of fine horses, to fight the Trojans. But tell me this, and tell me true. What death laid you low? Was it a long sickness, or did Artemis the archer come with her gentle arrows and bring you down? And tell me of my father, and of the son I left behind. Is my honor still safe in their hands, or has some other man taken it, thinking I will never come home? And tell me what my wedded wife intends, what is in her mind. Does she still hold to me and guard all that is mine — or has one of the Greeks, the best of them, married her by now?'

"And my honored mother answered me: 'She holds out still, her heart enduring, there in your halls. Her nights and her days waste away in sorrow and weeping. No man has yet taken your fine kingship; Telemachus holds your lands in peace and sits at the feasts a man who deals out justice is asked to share, for everyone invites him. But your father stays out in the country and never comes to town. He has no bed now, no blankets, no bright coverlets. In winter he sleeps in the house where the servants sleep, in the ashes by the fire, with poor rags on his body. And when summer comes and the rich harvest-time, he lies anywhere on the ground on the slope of his vineyard, on fallen leaves, grieving, nursing the sorrow in his heart, longing for you to come — and a hard old age has come on him. That is how I too died and met my fate. It was not the keen-eyed archer Artemis who shot me down with her gentle arrows in my own halls, nor any sickness that wastes the body and drains the spirit away. It was longing for you, my glorious Odysseus — your kindness and your counsel — that took the sweet life out of me.'

"So she spoke, and I longed in my heart to hold the spirit of my dead mother. Three times I started toward her, my whole heart aching to take her in my arms; three times she slipped through my hands like a shadow, like a dream. And the grief in me grew sharper, and I spoke to her, my words flying: 'Mother, why won't you stay for me, when I long to hold you — so that even here in the house of Hades we might throw our arms around each other and take some cold comfort in our shared sorrow? Is this only some phantom that dread Persephone has sent me, to make me weep and grieve all the more?'

"And my honored mother answered: 'Oh my child, unluckiest of all men born — Persephone, the daughter of Zeus, is not deceiving you. This is the way of mortals when they die. The sinews no longer hold the flesh and the bones together; the strong fury of the burning fire destroys all that, as soon as the life leaves the white bones, and the soul flutters off like a dream and is gone. But hurry back to the light now, with all speed. And keep all this in mind, so you may tell it to your wife in the days to come.'

"So we two spoke together. And then the women came — for dread Persephone drove them up to me, all the wives and daughters of the great men of old. They crowded around the dark blood, and I wondered how I might question them each in turn. This seemed the best plan: I drew the long sword from beside my sturdy thigh and would not let them all drink the dark blood at once. So they came up one by one, and each told me her birth, and I questioned them all.

"The first I saw was high-born Tyro, who said she was the daughter of faultless Salmoneus and the wife of Cretheus, son of Aeolus. She had fallen in love with a river, the god Enipeus, far the loveliest of the rivers that run on the earth, and she used to walk by his beautiful waters. There Poseidon, who holds and shakes the earth, took the river's shape and lay with her where the eddying stream runs into the sea. A dark wave reared over them, high as a mountain, curving to hide the god and the mortal woman. He loosed her maiden girdle and shed sleep over her. And when the god had finished the work of love, he took her by the hand and said: 'Be glad, woman, of this love. As the year comes round you will bear glorious children, for the bed of a god is never barren. Care for them and raise them. Now go home, and hold your tongue, and tell no one — for know that I am Poseidon, the Earthshaker.' With that he sank beneath the heaving sea. And she conceived and bore Pelias and Neleus, who both grew to be strong servants of mighty Zeus — Pelias rich in flocks, living in spacious Iolcus, and Neleus in sandy Pylos. And to Cretheus this queen of women bore others: Aeson, and Pheres, and Amythaon who fought from his chariot.

"After her I saw Antiope, the daughter of Asopus, who boasted she had slept in the very arms of Zeus, and bore him two sons, Amphion and Zethus. They were the first to found the seat of seven-gated Thebes and to wall it round, for strong as they were, they could not hold open Thebes without its walls. Next I saw Alcmene, the wife of Amphitryon, who lay in the arms of great Zeus and bore unconquerable, lion-hearted Heracles; and Megara, daughter of proud Creon, whom the tireless son of Amphitryon took as his wife.

"And I saw the mother of Oedipus, lovely Epicaste, who in the blindness of her heart did a monstrous thing — she married her own son. He had killed his own father, and married her, and the gods soon made it known to men. Yet for all his anguish he went on ruling the Thebans in their lovely land, by the cruel design of the gods; but she went down to the house of Hades, the strong gatekeeper, when she had knotted a high noose to a beam and hanged herself, mastered by her grief — and she left him agonies past counting, all that a mother's avenging Furies bring to pass.

"And I saw beautiful Chloris, whom Neleus once married for her beauty, after he had paid a fortune in bride-gifts. She was the youngest daughter of Amphion, son of Iasus, who once ruled with power in Minyan Orchomenus. She was queen in Pylos and bore him splendid children — Nestor, and Chromius, and lordly Periclymenus — and besides them she bore stately Pero, a wonder to all who saw her, whom every man around courted. But Neleus would give her only to the man who could drive off the cattle of mighty Iphicles from Phylace — a heavy task. A faultless seer alone promised to do it, but a god's harsh fate bound him fast, and the rough herdsmen and their chains. Yet when the months and the days had run their course and the seasons came round again, mighty Iphicles set him free, once he had told out all the oracles. And so the will of Zeus was done.

"And I saw Leda, the wife of Tyndareus, who bore him two strong-hearted sons — Castor, breaker of horses, and Polydeuces, mighty with his fists. The living earth holds them both, and yet they live: even under the ground Zeus gives them honor. One day they live and the next day they are dead, each in his turn, and they have won honor like the gods'.

"After her I saw Iphimedeia, the wife of Aloeus, who said she had lain with Poseidon. She bore two sons, but their lives were short — godlike Otus and far-famed Ephialtes, the tallest men the grain-giving earth ever raised, and the most beautiful by far, after famous Orion. At nine years old they were nine cubits across and nine fathoms tall, and they threatened to bring the roar of raging war up to the immortals on Olympus. They strained to pile Mount Ossa on Olympus, and leafy Pelion on Ossa, to make a stairway into heaven — and they would have done it, had they only reached the full measure of their strength. But the son of Zeus, whom fair-haired Leto bore, destroyed them both before the first down ever curled on their cheeks or covered their chins with a young beard.

"And I saw Phaedra, and Procris, and lovely Ariadne, the daughter of merciless Minos, whom Theseus once carried off from Crete toward the high ground of sacred Athens — but he had no joy of her, for first Artemis killed her on sea-girt Dia, on the word of Dionysus. And I saw Maera, and Clymene, and hateful Eriphyle, who took gold as the price of her own husband's life.

"But I could never name them all, all the wives and daughters of heroes that I saw; the immortal night would run out first. It is time now to sleep, whether I go down to the swift ship and the crew, or stay here. My setting-out will be in your hands, and the gods'."

So he spoke, and they all sat hushed and still, held in a spell through the shadowy hall. Then white-armed Arete was the first to break the silence: "Phaeacians, what do you think of this man — his looks, his stature, the steady mind within him? He is my own guest, but every one of you shares the honor of it. So do not be in a hurry to send him on, and do not stint your gifts to a man in such great need. You have many treasures in your halls, by the gods' good grace."

Then the old hero Echeneus spoke up, the eldest among the Phaeacians: "My friends, what our wise queen says is not wide of the mark or far from our own thinking — so do as she says. But the word and the work both rest with Alcinous here."

And Alcinous answered him: "Then let it stand as she has said, as surely as I am alive and rule over the Phaeacians who love the oar. Let our guest, for all his longing to be home, hold on until tomorrow, until I have made the whole gift ready. His passage will be the care of all of us, and mine most of all, for the power in this land is mine."

And Odysseus, the man of many turns, answered him: "Lord Alcinous, most renowned of all your people — if you bade me wait here even a whole year while you readied my passage and your splendid gifts, I would gladly do it. It would be far better to reach my own dear country with fuller hands; I would be more honored, more loved, by every man who saw me come home to Ithaca."

And Alcinous answered him: "Odysseus, looking at you, we do not take you for a cheat or a liar, the kind the dark earth breeds in such numbers, men who spin lies out of nothing a man could ever see. There is a grace on your words, and a sound mind within, and you have told your tale with the skill of a singer — the heavy sorrows of yourself and all the Greeks. But tell me this now, and tell me true. Did you see any of your godlike companions there, who went with you to Troy and met their fate? The night is long, beyond all measure; it is not yet time to sleep in the hall. Tell me these wonders. I could hold out until bright dawn, if only you were willing to go on telling me your sorrows here."

And Odysseus, the man of many turns, answered him: "Lord Alcinous, most renowned of all your people — there is a time for long telling, and a time for sleep. But if you still long to hear, then I will not hold back from telling you of things still more pitiful than these — the sorrows of my companions who died afterward, who came safe out of the Trojans' bitter war only to die on their return, by the will of a wicked woman.

"When holy Persephone had scattered the spirits of the women this way and that, there came the grieving spirit of Agamemnon, the son of Atreus, and around him gathered all the others who had died with him in the house of Aegisthus, meeting their fate there. He knew me at once, when he had drunk the dark blood. He wept aloud, the warm tears falling, and reached out his arms to me, longing to hold me — but the strength was gone, the firm power that had once filled his supple limbs. I wept when I saw him, and pity went through my heart, and I spoke to him, my words flying: 'Most glorious son of Atreus, Agamemnon, lord of men — what fate of pitiless death brought you down? Did Poseidon raise a dreadful blast of cruel winds and break you on the sea? Or did enemies cut you down on dry land while you were rounding up their cattle and fine flocks, or fighting for their city and their women?'

"And he answered me at once: 'Royal son of Laertes, Odysseus of the many turns — no, Poseidon did not break me on the sea with a blast of cruel winds, and no enemies cut me down on dry land. It was Aegisthus who plotted my death and my doom — he and my own accursed wife. He asked me to his house, he feasted me, and he killed me as a man kills an ox at its manger. So I died, the most pitiable death, and around me my companions were slaughtered without mercy, like white-tusked pigs cut down for a wedding feast or a banquet in a rich man's house. You have seen many men killed, in single combat and in the press of battle — but your heart would have ached most of all to see how we lay among the wine-bowls and the laden tables, all through the hall, and the whole floor running with blood. The most pitiful cry I ever heard was the voice of Cassandra, Priam's daughter, whom treacherous Clytemnestra killed at my side. I lifted my hands and beat the ground as I died with the sword in me; but the brazen-faced woman turned away and would not, though I was on my way to Hades, close my eyes with her hands or shut my mouth. There is nothing more dreadful, nothing more shameless, than a woman who can set her heart on a deed like this — as she did, plotting that monstrous thing, the murder of the husband of her youth. I thought I would come home to the welcome of my children and my servants — but she, with her heart bent on utter evil, has poured shame on herself and on all the women yet to be born, even on one who does what is right.'

"And I answered him: 'It is true — far-thundering Zeus has always borne a terrible hatred against the line of Atreus, working through the schemes of women. For Helen's sake so many of us died, and Clytemnestra laid her trap for you while you were far away.'

"And he said: 'So you too — never be soft, even with your own wife. Do not tell her everything in your mind. Tell her one thing, and keep the rest hidden. And yet you, Odysseus, will not be murdered by your wife — Penelope, Icarius' daughter, is too wise, too sound of heart for that. We left her a young bride when we marched off to war, with an infant at her breast, a boy who must be sitting now among grown men. Lucky child — his father will come home and see him, and he will throw his arms around his father, as a son should. But my wife would not even let me feast my eyes on my own son; she killed me first. And here is one more thing — take it to heart. Bring your ship in to your own dear land in secret, not in the open, for there is no trusting women anymore. But tell me this now, and tell me true — have you heard anything of my son, still living? In Orchomenus, perhaps, or sandy Pylos, or with Menelaus in broad Sparta? For surely my Orestes is not yet dead and gone.'
"And I answered him: 'Son of Atreus, why ask me this? I do not know whether he is alive or dead, and it is a poor thing to speak words into the wind.'

"So we two stood trading our sad words, grieving, the warm tears falling. And then there came the spirit of Achilles, son of Peleus, and the spirits of Patroclus and faultless Antilochus and of Ajax, who in build and in beauty was the finest of all the Greeks after the matchless son of Peleus. The spirit of the swift-footed grandson of Aeacus knew me, and grieving he spoke to me, his words flying: 'Royal son of Laertes, Odysseus of the many turns — reckless man, what greater thing than this could your heart still devise? How did you dare come down to Hades, where the dead live on without their wits, the worn-out husks of men who have done with their labor?'

"And I answered him: 'Achilles, son of Peleus, far the strongest of all the Greeks — I came needing Tiresias, to see if he could tell me any way to reach rocky Ithaca. For I have not yet come near Greece, nor set foot on my own land. I have nothing but trouble. But you, Achilles — no man was ever more blessed than you, nor ever will be. While you lived we Greeks honored you like a god, and now that you are here you rule with great power among the dead. So do not grieve at your dying, Achilles.'

"And he answered me at once: 'Don't gild death for me, glorious Odysseus. I would rather be a hired hand, working another man's land — a man with no portion of his own, scraping by — and be alive, than be lord over all the wasted dead. But tell me of my son, my proud boy. Did he follow the war as a leader, or not? And tell me of faultless Peleus, if you have heard — does he still keep his honor among the Myrmidons, or do they scorn him now through Hellas and Phthia, because old age has him by the hands and feet? For I am no help to him under the sun's light, the man I was on the wide plain of Troy, when I cut down the best of their army defending the Greeks. If I could come, even for a moment, to my father's house with that strength still in me, I would give any man who shames him and bars him from his honor good reason to dread these hands of mine.'

"And I answered him: 'Of faultless Peleus I have heard nothing. But of your dear son Neoptolemus I will tell you all the truth, as you ask. It was I myself who brought him over from Scyros in my trim, hollow ship, to join the well-greaved Greeks. Whenever we held council before Troy, he was always the first to speak, and he never missed the mark; only godlike Nestor and I outdid him.
